subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today reads, and I quote:
That this House condemn the Government for failing to honour the Prime Minister's promise to "double Canada's spending commitment to research and development".
Seven years ago next week, on March 22, 1984, the Prime Minister, speaking before the Montreal Chamber of Commerce, promised, and I quote: "-to double the collective national effort in the field of research and development during our first mandate".
Supply
He added, and I quote: "Through this effort, we expect to create hundreds of thousands of new jobs and increase overall sales by several billions of dollars each year".
It is not often, Mr. Speaker, that we, Liberals, agree with the Prime Minister's ideas. However, I can say flat out that we agree totally with those he expressed seven years ago about the importance of increased investment in research and development. Therefore, it is only logical that, today, we condemn the government and the Prime Minister for not delivering on this promise. We remember that, in his book entitled Where I Stand, the Prime Minister stated, and I quote: "Research and development, and the resulting innovations, are the lifeblood of a successful economy and country". The Prime Minister believed that, if the percentage of gross national product allocated to research and development were increased by a mere 1 per cent, we could create in Canada one million new jobs and $20 billion in additional sales of manufactured products.
We know what has happened since 1984: Spendings for research and development, instead of increasing, decreased by 1.4 per cent to 1.3 per cent of the gross national product. That was due to a reduction in the overall support to the research and development effort in Canada, and I can give you examples of that.
First, the Conservative government cut back on the support to industrial research and development. For instance, first-rate purchasing programs have been cancelled and the National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program is always starved for funds.
Second, the government reduced post-secondary education transfer payments and vocational training appropriations.
Third, the government went after Canada's foremost research agency-the National Research Council-and cut down the budget for research projects on environment and alternate energy sources.
Fourth, it cut in half the budget of the Science Council of Canada.
Fifth, intent on promoting university research, the government created the Centres of Excellence Program, yet at the same time it froze the funding of the main source of financial support for Canadian university research, the federal grants councils. The Prime Minis-

March 14, 1991
Supply
ter did not follow the recommendations of his own national advisory council which had advocated doubling the appropriations of grants councils.
Sixth, health care research was the latest victim of conservative restraints, including programs on health care research, health promotion, prevention of diseases-cancer, for one-as well as labour injuries and accidents.

Mr. Speaker, I anticipate that in their remarks today members of the government-and I see that the Minister for Science is here- will down-play the significance of research and development. They will say that research and development is a measure of input, that doing research and development does not necessarily lead to jobs and sales.
It is true that there is not as direct a link between R and D and jobs and sales, as the Prime Minister led people to believe in his remarks some seven years ago. Investment in research and development is needed but not sufficient for jobs and sales. It is also true that a company is not likely to increase sales without doing research and development. That becomes more and more so with advanced technology, goods and services. In theory, a bad firm can spend money on R and D and get nothing from it. Yet all successful firms spend a lot on research and development and get a lot from it.
Of course, Canada's major competitors routinely spend twice as much as Canada does on their R and D investments. Are they all stupid? Are they throwing billions of dollars away for nothing? The new products, all the technological improvements that we see every day have to come from somewhere, and that is from research and development.
Increasing spending on R and D is part and parcel of developing in Canada a research and development culture or a culture which values knowledge and education, and which would place top priority on developing Canada's human resources. Developing an R and D culture means giving Canadians the opportunities they deserve to attain their potential, to have meaningful choices for a variety of kinds of employment without
having to leave Canada to pursue a rewarding career in science or in research.
In the budget the finance minister announced that the government will launch, and I quote: "a national effort to build a new partnership for prosperity". As a first step he said, and again I quote: "We will release a discussion paper in the spring to help focus public debate about the problems we face and the development of solutions". The Minister of Finance said that "more needs to be done to assure our future prosperity. We need to look hard at the quality of our investments and infrastructure, machinery and equipment, training and education, and research and technology". "There are signs", the Minister of Finance says, "that in some areas, such as private sector research and development and training, we are not doing enough".
My reaction on hearing these remarks of the Minister of Finance was, this is news to the Minister of Finance. For 10 years now members of Parliament have heard from countless sources that we are falling behind in all the areas that he identified in his budget speech two weeks ago. From university teachers, presidents and students, from business executives and workers, union leaders and from the government's own advisory committees the case has been made eloquently and consistently and now seven years after the government took office it proposes to focus public debate on these questions.
Where has the government been for the past seven years? Has it not been the government's responsibility to take action in these areas, to show leadership, to develop the kind of research and development culture that I said earlier values knowledge, education and the development of our human resources?
The debate the government proposes to engage Canadians in coming months is an admission of failure, an admission that we have lost seven years when we should have taken steps to ensure that all Canadians receive quality education and that Canadians businesses do enough R and D.
John Polanyi, the University of Toronto chemist who in 1986 won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry, said shortly after being awarded that prestigious prize, and I quote:
Speaking from the perspective of someone who's been famous for
almost 24 hours, I have found that good research is a combination
of good luck, good colleagues, good students and adequate facilities.
March 14, 1991

The first, he said, comes from God; the rest from a university system properly supported by the government. Polanyi concluded:
I wonder whether we aren't relying rather more heavily on God
these days than on government.
Canadians need a government that will do its share.

It was not our government that threw the baby out with the bath water, it was his. He has got us into this situation now where the provinces have complete carte blanche to do what they want. I am glad that my hon. friend is learning that we need to support industrial research in this country. I will give him more figures on that this morning. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1984, the Prime Minister promised Canadians that he would undertake to double Canada's level of research and development.
This promise was reiterated at Halifax when he spoke to a Conservative gathering on June 19, 1989. He said to all Canadians that "Canada's place in the world is not guaranteed; either we meet the challenge of competitiveness and ride the crest of the technology wave into the 21st century, or we exhaust ourselves in the rip-tide of history, fading inexorably backward."
Beautiful words. I commend the Prime Minister on his eloquence, but we are here today to hold his feet to the fire. What is his promise? We have heard it. What has he done? The facts show just the opposite.

March 14, 1991
Supply
When the Conservative government took over running Canada in 1984, our level of R and D was 1.42 per cent of the gross domestic product. Every year, under his stewardship, it has fallen so that today it is at 1.28 per cent of gross domestic product. We are at less than one-half the level of all our major competitors.

For example, let us look at what they did to the National Research Council Canada, NRCC. Since 1984 the federal government has reduced its NRCC appropriations by 12 per cent, or more than $5.7 million. In constant dollars this reduction would amount to roughly 48 per cent.
Last year the government appointed Pierre Perron President of the National Research Council. When he appeared before our committee at that time I asked him whether he thought his role as head of Canada's premier research and development agency was to lead the scientific community or to do the government's bidding. He was miffed, he said, so I had to rephrase my question: Well, Mr. Perron, do you think your role as president should be to fight against the government's NRC cutbacks? He replied: No, I cannot do that.
That is what I call doing the government's biding without question. And just a few days ago, Mr. Speaker, we learned that sixty-odd important employees had to resign. The NRC spirit has been flattened by this government.
And that is not all. Is the government really intent on promoting science and technology? Mr. Speaker, budget increases for science and technology amount to a mere 3 per cent. That is much less than the inflation rate and it spells fewer grants and less support for the NRC.
With respect to education in Canada we have only 90 scientists and researchers per 100,000 inhabitants. That compares with 140 in Britain, 150 in West Germany, 240 in Japan, and 280 in the United States. As to federal transfers to the provinces for health and education between 1986 and 1995, the cut-backs of this government will translate into a $40.1 billion loss for the provinces.
This has now become a serious issue. Even the Minister of Finance acknowledged in his budget that it is
a matter of competitiveness for Canada. The World Economic Forum has shown that Canada lags far behind in terms of international competitiveness-down from fourth to fifth rank last year. -In research and development we are sixth among 24 industrialized countries, and that explains why we have so many bankruptcies in Canada, why our country is being de-industrialized.
Over the past 26 months Canada lost 277,000 manufacturing jobs, a frightening figure which accounts for 13 per cent of all jobs in the manufacturing sector. There is a direct link between this government's lack of support and the vanishing jobs in that major sector.
In the few minutes I have left I should like to comment on the recommendations of the Committee on Industry, Science and Technology. The report was drafted and endorsed by all three parties, and government members made up the majority of the committee. Here are some of the recommendations. We should raise the level of research and development. But this government has done nothing. In three years we were to double the budgets of three research councils, namely the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Social Sciences and Humanitys Research Council of Canada, and the Medical Research Council of Canada. The recommendation was to double appropriations over three years. What did they do in the budget? They limited government support to 3 per cent, which amounts to a loss in constant dollars.
The Science Council of Canada budget was to be brought up to the previous level of $5 million, but the SCC will have to make do with only $3.2 million. Our recommendation was an immediate boost to $100 million for IRAP-Industrial Research Assistance Program- but the budget has been kept down to only $85 million.
The committee recommended that the federal government reduce the renewal rate of these programs and staff for industry. We can see what they did with the National Research Council Canada. And then the government took $55 million off the total industry, science and technology budget.
Mr. Speaker, de-industrialization is creating a major problem. The only way to create sound manufacturing industries is to reverse these trends and double our efforts for science and technology and research and
March 14, 1991

development. The government is headed in the wrong direction, it needs to be set straight!

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues across the way but for quite different reasons, I am sure, I am delighted to participate in this debate today.
Hon. members of the Liberal party are quite right when they say that science and technology are crucial to the future of the Canadian economy. That is a message that cannot be repeated often enough. It is a truism, but one that I and many of my colleagues have been crossing the country to deliver. Nothing could please me more than to see it discussed in the House today.
We take very seriously our commitment to science and technology. At a time when we have had to cut back on government operations in order to fight a debt that will now reach almost $400 billion, the federal government has increased its R and D spending from $2.5 billion in 1984 to an estimated $3.2 billion in 1990. That is an increase of 28 per cent, while the government at the

March 14, 1991
Supply
same time has been under expenditure restraint trying to bring the economy of this country under control.
Total federal science and technology expenditures amounted to approximately $5.5 billion in 1990-91. Those expenditures on science and technology have increased in real terms by 8 per cent since 1984, by an average above inflation of 1.1 per cent each year since taking office. That is not too bad.
Our spending on science and technology grew from 11.1 per cent of all discretionary spending in 1984-85 to 12.3 per cent in 1990-91. That is the true indication of the priority that the government awards to spending on science and technology. This, I might add, is in contrast to the record of the previous government.
I would suggest to this House that these figures demonstrate a strong federal commitment to science and technology in Canada.
Hon. members opposite would like us to do more. We would all like to do more, certainly I would, but the strength of the Canadian economy does not depend solely upon science and technology.
Canada's performance in research and development does not take place in some sterilized atmosphere in some test tube. It takes place in a real world which is influenced by all kinds of important factors. The strength of the economy depends upon the availability of capital, the accessibility of international markets, the value of our dollar, and the general climate for business in the country. We cannot separate science and technology from any of those components.
Each of those factors is strongly influenced by the public debt in Canada, a debt that has been growing since 1970 and a debt that we must get under control.
As the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech a couple of weeks ago, "the interest on the debt alone this year is going to be $43 billion". Just compare that to what we are able to spend in terms of science and technology. The amount we spend in interest payments is eight times what we can afford to pay for all the federal R and D and related science activities.
Think of what we could do with that $43 billion for the granting councils, for the National Research Council, more for big science and little science, for small business involved in the leading edge of the high technology
revolution, and more scholarships to young people-all of the things that members of this House want to do, but we cannot do them in the range we wish unless we also take steps to control government spending.
I have lots of favourite programs, as has every member of this House, of the things we might like to do, but we cannot do them if we cannot pay down the debt. We cannot do them if we are spending $43 billion a year just to pay the interest on the debt.
In contrast to some of my colleagues on the other side of the House, I congratulate the finance minister for his budget. He has set us on a real course of fiscal responsibility. He has set us on a course where we will be able down the road to do all the things we want to do. In terms of science and technology, we have always had preferential treatment in every budget that this government has brought down; not as much as I would have liked, but we have always had top priority. I believe that is as it should be.
If finance ministers a decade ago had used fiscal restraint but at the same time had delivered a priority to science and technology, we would be in far better shape today. There is no question about that. We have to tighten our belts, but we recognize the critical role that science and technology plays in the economy.
The recent budget placed expenditure controls on many programs. My colleagues opposite scoff that science and technology, beginning in 1992-93, will receive increases of 3 per cent. When I look at what has happened to other government programs and the way we have to exercise that restraint, I know the Minister of Finance has given us a top priority. That is important. If members opposite would look at the situation realistically, they would agree that the government has done quite well in terms of science and technology operating in these difficult times.
People should know that the Government of Canada by itself cannot change the attitude of industry in terms of promoting more research and development. We cannot shoulder the financial burden. It has to be shouldered by Canadian industry; it has to be shouldered with the provinces, with the universities. When hon. members opposite refer to GERD, gross expenditures

March 14, 1991

on research and development over GDP-and I heard them on many occasions-we have to be very precise in our analysis of the problem. It is not what governments spend, because we compare with most of our competitors in terms of what governments spend. It is what industry in Canada has not found itself able to spend, and that is where we lose out with respect to other countries.
Canada's ratio of gross domestic expenditure on research and development to GDP is 1.35. The ratio in the United States is 2.86, and in Japan it is 2.72. It is an interesting figure to have and points out once again where the funding must come from, where the impetus must come from, if we are going to move forward. I agree with hon. members, and always have, that this is a disturbing situation. But the way to improve the ratio is not to pour more Government of Canada money into science and technology; it is to encourage industry to do more, to devise programs that will allow them to do more.
Incidentally, concentrating on the GERD is in fact only looking with one eye at what industrial people need in this country. It is equally important to concentrate on the amount of technology inflow that we need, as well as the R and D that we need. It is useful to open both eyes and look at both sides of this question.
We compare favourably in terms of civil expenditures. We are about the middle of the pack in terms of public sector spending on research and development. We spend more as a percentage of GDP than does the United States or Britain in terms of civil research; less than France, Sweden and the Netherlands; and about the same as Japan and Italy. Where we fall behind is in our private sector.
When we look at the ratio between industrial and public sector civil R and D we notice once again that Canadian research and development is very heavily dependent upon taxpayers' dollars. That has to change. The ratio in Japan between taxpayers' dollars and industrial dollars is something like 4.38; in France, 1.38; and in United States, 3.13. We have all these figures.
Sweden, in spite of its reputation as a socialist nation, is well ahead of Canada in terms of private sector spending in research and development. Its ratio is 2.49. Again, it points out what we have to do in Canada:
Supply
increase the amount of industrial research. That is the challenge and it is clear.

The difference between my colleagues opposite and the government is that we are not just going to say if the private sector increases the amount of research and development, everybody has to increase it by x per cent. We do not know whether that is appropriate or not. We do not know whether some sectors would be far better off to spend their money on technology inflow to adopt and adapt new technologies rather than invest significantly in R and D.
In our opinion there is only one way to go, and that is to do the analysis of the Canadian economy sector by sector and see what the problems are, why they do not invest in R and D, or indeed even if they should. That is one of the contracts we have given to the Science Council of Canada. We expect some of those results will be with us over the next few months.
The solution, as I have said, is not to replace private sector spending with public spending. That has been the record of our country now for 25 years. It does not work, and it is not going to work. We must get the private sector involved.
What can the government do to encourage more private sector R and D? For one thing maybe not generally known-and it certainly would not be known to some of my colleagues opposite-we have created one of the most favourable tax regimes in the world for private sector R and D. We do not say that. A recent Conference Board of Canada study put Canada's support for R and D through the tax system ahead of that of the United States, Britain, Japan, Korea, France, Italy, Sweden, West Germany and Australia. Australia's is probably very close to our own.
Canada's tax system for research and development consists of two main features. First, the ability to write off fully R and D current capital expenditures in the year the costs occur. Second, R and D tax credits are used either to reduce a company's federal income tax liability or they are refunded in cash. The system helps start-up companies, particularly the small companies, get going. That is what we have done.

Canada's tax system-and the latest figures I have are for 1988-was responsible for $764 million in tax credits. That is a substantial contribution to $3.4 billion invested by business that particular year. What is more, 65 per cent of the claims came from small and medium sized businesses, which is the kind of business we are hoping to promote.
Indeed, we have even met with the industries, sector by sector, again to ask: "Does the income tax system work well for you? Is the R and D system working well? What problems do you have? " We have sat down again with Revenue Canada and worked it out sector by sector to see what we could do.
Those things take time. They are not things that are on the front page of the newspaper, but they are the things that will make Canadian industry grow and that is why we are doing them.
Look at the initiatives that we have launched. I do not need to repeat the networks of centres of excellence; 500 researchers at 35 universities and 37 other research bodies all involved in these networks across Canada. That is the way to promote the interaction we need, $244 million to 15 networks. That is a significant amount. The strategic technologies program to promote networks and alliances are being led by industry itself. Forty of these alliance projects are now in place; 13 of them in advanced industrial materials, 20 in biotechnology, seven in the information technologies.
The Canada scholarship program is a massive acknowledgement that young men and women should be studying science and engineering today. That initiative came from the Government of Canada through the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology.
I want to take a moment to talk about the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology. It has been very influential in setting the science and technology policy for Canada since it was formed in 1987 with the Prime Minister in the chair. NAB ST is really responsible for the networks of centres of excellence. It is the one which came up with this idea.
NAB ST was really behind the Canada scholarship program and particularly the concept of allowing or insisting that 50 per cent of the scholarships go to women. NABST recognized that we are not going to
resolve the people problem of Canada unless we can somehow encourage and recruit more young women to science and engineering. NABST was the one which made that recommendation.
It was NABST that was behind the $1.4 billion to science and technology announced two or three years ago. In recent days, the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology has presented to the Prime Minister, and he was in the chair, the financing of industrial innovation, human resources development, and science, technology, innovation and national prosperity. Those recommendations had a significant influence upon the finance minister and the government's commitment to look again at the whole concept of an agenda for prosperity, using innovation and research and development.
I wanted to get those words in on the National Advisory Board because many of the members will be retiring from NABST after serving for three or four years. I wanted to acknowledge publicly their influence, not only upon government programs, but their influence upon government policy. They have had this constant interaction with the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the ministers of our department.
Let me conclude on a subject that has always been discussed in the House, and I think all members are very interested in it, and that is women in science and engineering. We heard from my hon. colleagues this morning how we had to do more about the people situation in Canada and we had to change attitudes. I have just a few things to add. Half of the Canada scholarships go to women. Corporate members, institutions and industries are now beginning to support mentor clubs and additional corporate funding for other kinds of scholarships, all hooked into the Canada scholarship program.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, recently the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council have made some interesting innovations. NSERC's policies are intended to encourage women to pursue graduate studies and research and to encourage universities to hire more women as faculty members. In the last competition they had so many good applicants by encouraging women to take faculty positions, that instead of offering 10 fellowships, they offered 20. They just had to do it because the applications were so good.

We have 200 new undergraduate student research awards by NSERC and just a couple of months ago the National Research Council announced that they have in fact a new summer program for women to work in their laboratories across Canada that will stimulate once again the interest of young men and young women in these things. They will go back to their own high schools. They will tell their colleagues and their young friends and their sisters and their brothers of the importance of science and technology.
We have done something about these things. We have had a large program. We have not stood idly by.

He knows very well that what I was doing was stating a simple statistical fact, that if the GERD goes down as a percentage of GDP and industry's contribution goes up then the government's contribution must be going down.
What is bad about it is that the debate is about the fact that this government promised to increase the gross expenditures on research and development, and it is doing it by cutting government expenditures. That is a hell of a way to meet a goal established by a Prime Minister.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a motion which draws the attention of this House and indeed of the people of Canada to a subject of prime concern.
There is no question that Canadians are deeply concerned about our ability to compete internationally in an increasingly global economy. The success of our efforts in greater international competition will depend of course in large measure on our ability to be more productive, particularly in the areas of research and development and in the training and retraining of our work force.
The increasing interdependence in the world means that all industrialized countries place increasing emphasis on research and development, on science and technology in the broadest sense, and indeed on the quality of education of their people.
In Canada we no longer have the possibility of hoping to achieve greater global competitiveness through reliance on our resource industries, industries which for many generations provided Canadians with a high standard of living, but which can no longer provide that level of living to Canadians. We are increasingly challenged by a global economy and by the higher technologies that emerge from such a global marketplace.
If Canada were to engage in protectionism there would be no solution to the questions of our future prosperity. The route we must go is of course to engage fully in the liberalized global trading economy. To do that, we must equip ourselves with the necessary higher technologies and improved human skills which will enhance our comparative advantages and our competitiveness.
The only way to increase our international competitiveness, as I mentioned a moment ago, is through improved productivity. In the high technology sector opportunities for increased productivity are the greatest. Quite obviously Canada should move aggressively into such areas especially as the Third World takes on the simpler forms of manufacturing and mass production. The impetus is there for Canada to engage in higher technology manufacturing and production processes.
It is past time in Canada that we gave more attention to the need for science and technology and for research and development. The current government, when it came to office in 1984, set itself a priority to define a new science and technology strategy. I am sure all Canadians would join me in regretting that, despite the high flown

March 14, 1991
Supply
statements of that period, the government did not make the progress it had set for itself.
Through a consultative process, a process which I am sure all of us would endorse, the government of the day did attempt to identify where it is that we could best develop science based innovation in the Canadian economy. Elowever, since setting itself that goal, it has not provided the incentives, the tax incentives in particular, that could have helped to make a reality of that policy initiative.
The centres for excellence which the government committed itself to establishing have not flourished. The networking of university, government and industry laboratories has not proceeded in anything like the way that it has proceeded in the countries with which Canada competes in the global markets to which I referred a moment ago. Canada, on the contrary, continues to fund and conduct its research and development at low levels.
For example, in recent years merely 100 companies accounted for 75 per cent of Canadian industrial research and development, with only 10 companies accounting for 40 per cent of that total. The situation in essence has not improved. The vast majority of Canadian businesses still does not conduct any research and development.
In those circumstances I would ask how it is that we think in Canada that we can keep up with state of the art technologies which are being developed among our principal trade partners.
I want to quote in that context a statement by the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, which three years ago noted:
Canada's-capacity to perform in industry strategic applied research-is appallingly weak-A strong capacity to perform longterm applied research is essential as part of our industrial structure, if strategic market opportunities are to be identified by industry and pursued through sound programs of investments keyed to all the elements in the chain of innovation.
That was the judgment of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research some three years ago. There is certainly no reason today to challenge that judgment. In fact, there is every reason to believe the situation has not
improved, despite the fact that the reduction in trade barriers including those in the United States-Canada Free Trade Agreement, make it all the more imperative that Canada's research and development capacities be fostered.
I am not one who would advocate that we merely throw money at science and technology. No such simplistic answer would meet Canadian circumstances. There is already some degree of research and development support in our country, although it is relatively low, but it really is the market success of the research upon which we should concentrate and industry should be encouraged to address.
Our traditional comparative advantage in resource industries, which I noted a few moments ago, may have made Canadian industry and indeed the Canadian government rather complacent, but certainly the time for complacency is long since passed, especially in light of the global trade liberalization which I have already touched upon.
It seems to me that the efforts of the government should in general be to develop a broad consensus on the need to improve our scientific and technological base and to identify and capitalize on strategic market opportunities. We should promote industrial consortia, groupings of industrial companies that can augment our capacity for long-term applied research. That too is an area where government incentive could be of great importance.
Equally important, the linkages among industry, university and government to train specialists and to aid in technology transfer could certainly be fostered through the increased privatization of government funded research. Such a policy, I might add, has been in the forefront of the recommendations of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce for sometime, as well as in the case of universities, and yet we have seen little action on the part of this government in that direction.
I would also suggest that we should expand the availability of private equity capital to finance smaller technology based companies. We should look again at the way in which we finance R and D through tax incentives and tax credits.
March 14, 1991

If this government were to pursue those policies, we would today have a much stronger research and development based industry with which to compete with others.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague on the other side for his as always very thoughtful comments about this issue.
He mentioned the Canadian Institute of Advanced Research and its preoccupation-and it is a good one- with the lack of pre-competitive research in Canada.
That is where we hurt. That is where we are having our difficulty. It is hard to get Canadian industries to co-operate with each other in that area. I like to mention the Sony-Philips consortium which did all of the precompetitive research for the compact disc. Then, when they realized they could in fact have a product, they went their own separate ways again.
It has been hard to get Canadian companies to accept that kind of philosophy, that kind of co-operation. That is why the networks of centres of excellence were established, to see if we could not bring those units together somehow.
The Strategic Technologies Program responds to some extent to my colleague's concern about industrial consortia. In that program we will provide 50 per cent of the funding for pre-competitive research, either in advanced industrial materials, the biotechnologies or the information technologies. It is a move in the direction that my friend has been talking about.
I think in terms of funding for start-ups and that kind of thing. I hope, when the latest National Advisory Board on Science and Technology reports are released within the next few weeks, that he would be kind enough to give me his personal comments on the issue of financing, which one of those reports does address in some detail. I know his interest and I know his expertise. I would be very grateful for his personal comments when we are able to deliver those reports to him.

I should be pleased, Mr. Speaker, to respond to the minister's kind suggestion. I certainly shall take the occasion to offer a few comments.
However, let me say at once that I recognize, as I believe he does, that part of the difficulty in this broad
area of research and development has been the degree to which foreign ownership has marked the manufacturing industry in particular.
We could, I suppose, engage in a debate today about the merits of previous governments' policies about promoting or indeed discouraging Canadian investment in Canada. However, the time is so limited I think I shall resist that temptation and merely suggest that any government action, and I hope the government would share this view, should be on the supply side, that it would and provide the circumstances through education, through tax incentives and other devices to encourage greater private sector activity. The government would not itself reach in, designate or select specific corporations where some funding might be thought to be of assistance. That would be of course a direct intervention on the part of the government.
I would instead urge this government to look again at its budgetary policies with regard to promoting the circumstances which can give rise to the enhanced growth of R and D in our country.

Mr. Speaker, the entire country has become more aware of the crisis problem of violence against women. Indeed, yesterday we debated the need for a royal commission.
For the past few months, the subcommittee on the status of women has been hearing testimony on the terrible and terrifying subject. But it is clear that not all legislators are as concerned with or as sensitive to this issue as we might wish. I refer to Ontario's Minister of Consumer and Corporate Relations, sunshine boy extra-

March 14, 1991
ordinaire, who has hired as his adviser on sexism a man convicted of assaulting his common law spouse.
Premier Rae's office said that Mr. Grimaldi has made his penance. While no one disagrees, I ask: "Is this the message that Bob Rae and the New Democrats want to send?"
This appointment is no joke. It is an affront to the women of Canada. Mr. Kormos and his cavorting demeans himself, his government and the profession of politics.

Mr. Speaker, according to a Decima poll released this week, 90 per cent of rural Canadians are satisfied with the results of Canada Post's rural conversion program.
Yet people are complaining of a reduction of service in towns like Dubuc in Saskatchewan where one person wrote to Canada Post saying: "We have no counter service at all on Mondays. Any emergency mailings have to be taken out of town even though we used to have counter service Monday through Saturday".
A person from Claremont, Ontario sent a letter to us to protest the closure of their post office. She says: "You just have not seen this the way the average Canadian resident does. We want our post office". These letters and many others in the same vein were also sent to the minister's office, but it seems he has chosen to ignore them.
The minister should know that polls do not always reflect reality, except maybe when it comes to evaluating the popularity of his party. But this is one exception.

Mr. Speaker, last Monday, I had the honour of addressing a group of Tibetan Canadians to celebrate the 1959 uprising in Lhassa.
It is true to say that the government of Canada does not recognize Tibet, but it is also true to point out that no Canadian government did since 1959.
However, I want to remind the Tibetan community that the government of Canada cares greatly for their fellow countrymen and women and did not hesitate to condemn the Chinese government in the UN, through the Canadian ambassador, Mr. Yves Fortier, who told the UN Human Rights Commission last November, and I quote:
We will continue criticizing the Chinese government for its breaches in the field of human rights. By proclaiming the concern of the people of Canada for the respect of basic human rights in China, we are not trying to isolate that country. We believe that we are encouraging China, by keeping it in contact with ideas from abroad, to start up again the reform process launched ten years ago.
We are hoping, Mr. Speaker, that this would allow Tibet to regain freedom.

Mr. Speaker, we had an opportunity, yesterday, to hear what the President of the United States had to say about the political status of Canada and particularly the exaggerated interpretation given by the Prime Minister of Canada.
I think that, if it was unacceptable for De Gaulle to come and state his views of the Canadian and Quebec political environment in the 1960s, it is equally unacceptable for the President of the United States to interfere today in the internal affairs of Canada.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we hope that the President of the United States will have seen through the Prime Minister and, in the future, apply a strict non-interference policy regarding Canadian internal affairs.

Mr. Speaker, in my riding, we are very proud to have a higher than average population of veterans.
We are naturally pleased at the positive attitude taken by the Minister of Veterans Affairs last week when he indicated that services to veterans and their families will not be affected by the budget and spending restraints. The minister is confident that his staff and officials can meet the fiscal restraint as an opportunity and management challenge. Just as private industry has been required to cut its cloth to fit today's competitive times, so
March 14, 1991

the Public Service is more than capable of adjusting to the new realism.
The Department of Veterans Affairs plays a very important role in Cumberland-Colchester, and I appreciate the minister's firm stand and the support of his department.

Canada's only fax machine manufacturer, the Widecom Group of Mississauga, has recently been recognized by the Guinness Book of Records for developing the world's largest facsimile machine.
This new product will allow for the first time the transmission of blueprints, engineering drawings and other oversized documents. Three years of privately funded research by Widecom will create many new jobs in Mississauga and help the Canadian economy when manufacturing escalates to meet foreign demand.
This government should learn from high technology companies like Widecom and reverse its decision to cap funding to science and technology and post-secondary education. The future of Canada should be given more credit.

Mr. Speaker, for more than ten years, the whole eastern part of Canada, particularly the Eastern Townships in Quebec, have been plagued with the very serious problem of acid rains. The maple groves of Tingwick, Ham-Nord and Disraeli, in my beautiful riding of Richmond-Wolfe are economically very important for farmers and producers. The same can be said about deciduous and coniferous forests that are unfortunately suffering also from those acid rains.
The signing of a treaty between Mr. Mulroney and Mr. Bush in Ottawa yesterday fortunately ensures our environment will be saved and preserved since the treaty lays down precise rules regarding maximum levels of emissions. It also forces both parties to cooperate closely in environmental planning.
That is a tremendous gain for Quebec as well as the riding of Richmond-Wolfe, and it took only five years to achieve, while previous governments sat and did nothing about that for ten years.

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, nobody can support acts of vandalism like those that were perpetrated last Ihesday in Port-aux-Basques. But we have to understand the nub of the problems that led Newfoundland fishermen to resort to such measures.
Those fishermen are in a wedge, Mr. Speaker. While large foreign factory ships swallow up our fish stocks, their quotas are cut. High interest rates and new taxes increase their production costs.
And above that, the Minister of Fisheries is imposing this new burden on them: a wharf suveillance program for which the fishermen will have to pay themselves.
Mr. Speaker, Newfoundland fishermen see their standard of living taking a plunge and the Minister of Fisheries is slapping them in the face. That is why they are angry. If the Minister wants to avoid any more violence, he will have to stop ignoring the demands of the fishermen and start listening to them.

Mr. Speaker, two days ago I was pleased to mention in this House the good news with respect to the decontamination of different sites in Quebec because of the initiative taken by our government. But today, Mr. Speaker, we have one more reason to be happy since the Prime Minister and the President of the United States, Mr. Bush, have signed yesterday the long-awaited agreement on acid rain control and air quality.
Mr. Speaker, that is another of our government's tangible achievements in the environmental area. And that was made possible for both countries thanks to the dedication and never ending work of the Prime Minister, Mr. Brian Mulroney, who has been so determined as to

March 14, 1991
put forward an agreement that will benefit both our countries as well as future generations.
In the name of the people of my riding, I want to pay him a tribute today and I urge all members of this House to do the same because that is an important achievement for all Canadian men and women. Congratulations, Mr. Prime Minister!

After Michael Wilson's budget comes the deluge, Mr. Speaker. For Canadians depending on medicare, this has meant a deluge of proposed user fees, deinsuring of medical services, closure of hospital beds, and lay-offs of health personnel. Yesterday the Tory Nova Scotia minister of health suggested charging an annual premium for all Nova Scotians using medicare, similar to the premiums now levied by the Tory provinces of B.C. and Alberta.
This user fee would be in addition to the higher charges for such services as prescription drugs and children's dental care. All of these charges and fee increases flow directly from the five-year freeze on federal contributions to provincial medicare plans.
When asked how he will protect Canadians from the growing erosion of medical services, the minister of health and welfare always mentions the Canada Health Act. Nothing in that act stops the provinces from charging premiums, laying off health personnel, closing hospital beds or taking away services.
What the minister is really saying to low and middle income Canadians who depend on medicare is: "Let them eat cake".

Mr. Speaker,
I wish to draw to the attention of the House a very important and, for me, a most sentimental occasion which will take place on Parliament Hill next Monday, March 18.
Many on all sides of the House will remember with fondness the late Sean O'Sullivan, who was my predecessor as MP for Hamilton-Wentworth and, indeed, one of the youngest and finest members of Parliament ever to grace this Chamber.
Sean resigned his seat in 1977 and dared to become a priest with great distinction. He was appointed a member of the Order of Canada.
God took Father Sean from us in March 1989 at the age of 37 after a long battle with leukemia.
This House will commemorate Sean in a formal way. We passed a resolution in November 1990 that a sitting room at the Wellington Street entrance to the East Block be set aside as a meditation place for people of all faiths. This room, to all those who enter it, will forever be a reminder of God's special friend, Father Sean O'Sullivan.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday in my riding of Dartmouth at CFB Shearwater I had the pleasure of welcoming home some of the first of the Canadian men and women returning from the Persian Gulf.
These troops, from various Canadian forces bases, returned after proudly contributing to the successful efforts of freeing Kuwait from the oppression of Saddam Hussein.
These brave Canadian men and women are a model of strength and courage which all Canadians should greatly admire and respect. They placed their lives on the line in the name of Canada to preserve freedom and democracy, life and liberty, peace and humanity.
The remainder of their colleagues serving on the Terra Nova, the Athabaskan, and the Protecteur is steaming back toward Canada. I know, Mr. Speaker, that when their ships arrive in Halifax harbour, they will be witness to the gratitude and thanksgiving of all Canadians as tens of thousands of Nova Scotians will line the shores of Halifax harbour to say thank you and welcome home.
They have served us well but, more so, have caused us to reflect on how fortunate we all are to live in this great country, Canada. For their service and their example we say thank you and wish them a safe and speedy trip home.
March 14, 1991

Mr. Speaker, sustainable development, one of the most important issues in Canada and around the world, focuses on balancing economic concerns with environmental concerns.
In the pursuit of the goal of sustainable development, Canada's Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and American President George Bush signed the historic Canada-U.S. air quality accord.
This agreement sends an important signal to the world and demonstrates that a key element in achieving sustainable development is a determined spirit of co-operation, not only between countries but also between various levels of government, industry, the scientific community, and the public.
If we are to continue to address successfully the needs of our society, then we must work together to ensure that environmental goals are responsibly pursued in our efforts to meet the ever-increasing economic challenges.
Let us work together for a cleaner environment and a better quality of life for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, a woman in New York was just awarded $4.5 million after a jury ruled that a toxic substance released from the foam covering of a Meme breast implant caused cancer in that woman. They were amazed that a product which contains a known carcinogen would be implanted in women.
Canadian women are not protected from this. Since last April I have twice raised this issue in the House with the minister of health. I asked that he remove the product from the market until it was proven to be safe. He accused me of fearmongering.
The FDA in the U.S. has recently taken steps which would implement the strict regulation of breast implants. They will have to prove the safety and effectiveness of implants before they are allowed on the market.

now paying the price for that, will he assure us that he will take the first step necessary to promote economic recovery in Canada and give us a new Minister of Finance who an be trusted to handle this economic crisis?

I am not acquainted with all of the details of this. It would not strike me as being inappropriate that there would be a study on competitiveness done jointly with the Business Council on National Issues. If my hon. friend, in respect of the question which she raised which dealt with international competitiveness and enhancing Canada's productivity, is making a request for a grant to a specific organization to conduct such a study, we would be happy to look at it.

The hon. member knows it, and that was the aim of the motion, which is not a very noble goal. The leader of the New Democratic Party will have to recognize that.
As to her fundamental question, I mentioned several times- I don't know whether she has been traumatized, but every time she gets up she talks about the corporate elite.

What about the big labour elite? Why is the hon. member so traumatized by the corporate elite and so comfortable with big labour rules?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade. The minister told us today that he is trying to seek a consensus among the provincial premiers on the surtax on softwood lumber exports. He has said some provinces, notably New Brunswick, are against approaching the Americans.
The question I would like to ask is, what is the position of the federal government and what is the minister advising his provincial counterparts?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position of the government and my position is that matters have changed since 1986 when the countervail duty case was launched. There have been considerable changes since then. Several provinces have instituted new stumpage charges in their provinces, such as British Columbia and Quebec. There have been significant changes in the industry. Our dollar has appreciated 19.4 per cent. Our share of the U.S. market has dropped from 33 per cent to 27 per cent. So there have been very considerable changes.
Anyone who examines this question impartially and rationally will agree, I am sure, that the time has come for the memorandum of understanding to be done away with. However, we are not necessarily dealing with people who are rational or impartial. We are dealing with people like the hon. gentleman opposite. Therefore, it is not going to be easy to accomplish this. We have to assess the risks and the possible benefits, which we are now in the process of doing.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is to the same minister.
The 15 per cent surtax coupled with a high dollar policy have caused close to 100,000 job losses in the forestry industry. The minister has said that he wants to renegotiate the agreement, but the American Congress has said that it would not. Can the minister tell us what the government will do if the Americans refuse to negotiate? Will the government take some firm action
Oral Questions
on behalf of the tens of thousands who have already lost their jobs in the forestry industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the memorandum of understanding with reference to softwood lumber is not the only matter that has affected the softwood lumber industry. When we decide upon a course of action, I want the provinces-or most of them-supportive of that course of action. When I am out in front leading the charge down in Washington, I do not want them suddenly disappearing behind my back. That is the purpose of this consultation; to make sure we are united and agreed on the course of action we are going to follow through, no matter how tough it might be.

Mr. Speaker, with an unemployment rate of over 14 per cent and retail sales that dropped 20 per cent this month, Montreal has become the unemployment capital of Canada. With unemployment comes poverty. So much so that this year, 53,000 families are obliged to go to the Sun Youth Food Bank. This is a disgrace, and it also very sad. I therefore want to ask the Prime Minister what kind of programs the government is going to set up in Montreal to help these families get out of the poverty cycle and store their dignity?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree the economic situation in Montreal is difficult. We realize this and we sympathize with the people who are in this situation. However, it must be said that the government has done a great deal since 1984 for the Montreal area. We have invested hundreds of millions of dollars, and I could name a number of examples for the benefit of the hon. member for Mount Royal. Recently, the Minister of Science and Technology invested $112 million in one of the poorest areas in Montreal, and I am referring to the southwest. And we also set up a training centre for petrochemical workers in East Montreal. Since 1985, we have created 83,000 jobs in Montreal, and that is better than the previous Liberal government which lost 4,000.

March 14, 1991
Oral Questions

The ex-psychiatric people, the single parent families, the poor and the elderly are not interested in being statistics. These are human beings who are lining up at these food banks and need to be fed.

Even in my own riding of Mount Royal, a food bank and food aid are needed. Formerly, Multicaf used to distribute about 30 baskets per month. Now we are up to 350 baskets per month. This is a terrible human catastrophe. My supplementary is directed to the Prime Minister. In a country where we have a food surplus, I would like to know whether he is prepared to help food banks fill their shelves. And if not, who is going to feed the poor in our communities in Montreal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member when she says there are many poor people in Montreal. However, my colleague should also realize that since 1984, we helped 760,000 people in Canada rise above the poverty line. This is cold comfort for the people who are still living in poverty, but nevertheless, one-third of these people-the hon. member refered to children as well- one-third of those 760,000 people who are no longer living below the poverty line are children. So we have made progress in a number of other areas. In Montreal, for instance, the Space Agency has created jobs. The Liberal party tried to kill the petrochemical industry in Montreal but the Prime Minister rescued it. It is true Montreal has problems, but this Conservative government has done a lot for Montreal.

My question is to the Minister of the Environment. On November 18, 1987, the Prime Minister and President Reagan signed an agreement on Great Lakes water quality, which adopted
zero discharge of persistent toxic substances into the Great Lakes.
The principles of that agreement have never been enforced and the horrible effects of toxics are now seen on fish, wildlife and human health.
In fact there have been only seven pollution prosecutions in all of Canada under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act since 1988.
Would the minister explain why the government plans now to enforce zero discharge of toxics only in Lake Superior? Will that not turn other water bodies in Canada into toxic waste dumps?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind my colleague opposite that the government has acted very aggressively in terms of cleaning up the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River basin.
We are making progress both in the Great Lakes and in the St. Lawrence River with programs that total some $260 million. We will be moving in the very near future with the U.S. on a joint agreement in terms of further clean-up operations in the Great Lakes. We are moving very firmly to meet the commitment that we have made for the virtual elimination of toxic chemicals by the year 2000. We still maintain that we will move to zero discharge down the road.

Mr. Speaker, as of today, only seven of Canada's provinces are part of the national acid rain reduction program, while all the United States is covered by the 1990 U.S. clean air legislation, both National CAP and National Reduction Program.
Would the minister explain why last November 27 he said that the agreement of the three western provinces was necessary to make yesterday's acid rain accord fly?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is very simple.
I met all the members of the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment in Victoria. We discussed the issue thoroughly, and I got the agreement of all provinces to meet the goals of limiting emissions as we have stated in the agreement yesterday.
March 14, 1991

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Minister of Justice.
Members will know that the crisis which erupted last summer in Kanesatake and Kahnawake resulted basically over a land dispute. When the minister realized that this disputed land was destined to become a golf course, why did the minister not exercise his or her authority and bring in an immediate moratorium on the development of any land in dispute?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may, as my hon. colleague probably remembers, at the time of the dispute there had been negotiations with respect to that particular land in Oka.
The negotiations had been going on for about two years. As a former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development at the time, I had appointed negotiators to do that. Negotiations at the time were suspended by the new chief and council that had just been elected at that time.

Mr. Speaker, my question goes unanswered.
Basically, the acting minister will know that indeed the Government of Canada has myriad statutes available to it, providing expropriation powers that could have been exercised to diffuse the situation.
Having said that, testimony received last night from an environmental group provided unprecedented evidence that the land in question has historical environmental significance. This is supported by a petition of 1,200 names.
If this group considers it to be of such value that it would equal the status of a world heritage site, why then would the minister not exercise his or her authority and put on a moratorium?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I think everybody would agree here. The hon. member in particular should agree to the proposition that best way to settle land claims issues in this country is at the negotiating table.
Oral Questions
If the band and council had come to the negotiating table, as we were prepared to be there for over a year, it might have been settled then and would be settled now.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Last June the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick unanimously adopted legislation to enshrine the principles of Bill 88 which acknowledges the equality of both official linguistic communities in New Brunswick. Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member will recall that the constitutional agreement signed by the First Ministers in June 1990, when that legislation was adopted in New Brunswick, provided for two amendments to Bill 88.
One bilateral amendment provided for the enshrinement of the principle of equality of both linguistic communities in New Brunswick and the role of the provincial government as protector and promoter of that characteristic. As the hon. member will recall, the second amendment was to protect the contents of Bill 88 by preventing amendments without the unanimous agreement of the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick and of the federal Parliament.
Now since the second amendment, linked to the first, died with the Meech Lake failure, any over-all approach to the Bill 88 solution died right along with it. What the Governments of Canada and New Brunswick should do now would be to get together and consider the best way to achieve our common goal-Canada's and New Brunswick's-of enshrining Bill 88 in the Canadian Constitution.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to ask the Prime Minister this: Is the Prime Minister of Canada, through the minister who just answered, saying no to the Premier of New Brunswick who is asking, on behalf of Acadians from his province,

March 14, 1991
Oral Questions
for the entrenchment of Bill 88, as passed unanimously by the New Brunswick Legislative Assembly, an essential Act for the survival of Acadians in Canada, under the present circumstances.

On the
contrary, Mr. Speaker. I told the Premier of New Brunswick that we also wanted to see the rights of Acadians entrenched. That is one of the reasons why it was so important for all legislative assemblies to approve the Meech Lake Accord, because the entrenchment of those rights was directly related to this project. But unfortunately, it is also one of the reasons why the rights of an important majority, the Acadian people, were affected by all this.
As the minister just said, I have met the Premier of New Brunswick and we are working together to find means, and even constitutional means, to entrench and better protect the vital rights of the Acadians and French-speaking residents of New Brunswick.

I have a question for the Minister for International Trade, and I want to assure him that I am entirely rational and certainly impartial.
I want to point out to him that there are two sides to every story, and some members today have called for the government to drop the 15 per cent tax on softwood lumber. In Atlantic Canada we are very much opposed to such an action because it could have very damaging effects on an area of Canada that has really been an innocent bystander throughout this whole argument.
We seek the consensus of all the provinces or I understand you do. I want to ensure that all those provinces included all the Atlantic provinces, that you do not risk any countervail action through these negotiations and consider the concerns of Atlantic Canada in this very important issue.
What is your question?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is certainly the first rational question I have had today.
The fact we have to keep in mind is that 90 per cent of softwood lumber exports to the United States, valued at $2.6 billion in 1990, came basically from two major producing provinces, British Columbia and Quebec, and their concerns have to be paid close attention to by us.
I am aware of the views particularly of the industry and Governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
We have had three consultations with them. I will meet again tomorrow with the New Brunswick minister responsible for forestry and the acting minister of commerce and technology.
Everyone's views will be kept in mind, but there is one salient fact: 90 per cent of the softwood lumber exports, valued at $2.6 billion, are from these two provinces, British Columbia and Quebec. We simply cannot ignore their interests which are being seriously affected in this case.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General.

My question to the Solicitor General is simply this: Could he tell us whether CB Chemicals is one of those 12 companies that the Minister of Public Works cited as being under RCMP investigation?

speechtext:

When the hon. gentleman carps and brings this up in an attempt to embarrass the government or to embarrass individuals, he should keep that in mind.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very straightforward. I think the government does enough to embarrass itself.
My question is really veiy simple. If the Royal Canadian Mounted Police provide press releases by which we find out, for example, that Technitread is under RCMP investigation, then why can't the government come clean about those 12 RCMP investigations set out by the minister himself in the House of Commons, rather than wait for press releases from the RCMP?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, not only is the question very simple but so is the hon. member.
Oh, oh.

speechtext: Perhaps the hon. minister could answer the question.

With respect to this issue, some months ago the minister responsible for ACOA took the initiative with respect to the Enterprise Cape Breton operation to appoint a commissioner or a person to look into the operations of Enterprise Cape Breton, in the person of a Mr. Tony Brait.
There is no attempt to hide that there has been difficulty in certain instances in Atlantic Canada, but these are a very small proportion of the 7,600 applications. One wonders why the hon. member is carrying on a vendetta against Atlantic Canada with these questions.

speechtext:

In 1985, after a reduction in commercial interest rates, the Minister of Agriculture reduced the interest on Farm Credit Corporation loans from 14 per cent to 12.75 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
that logic is so wrong today, why was it so right in 1985?

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)

Mr. Speaker, that member was not around in 1981 and 1982 when the Farm Credit Corporation was forced to charge interest rates way above what we have now.
I happen to have been a farmer and a member then and know what kind of damage the policies of that government did to the agricultural community. We are still trying to recover from them.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister for International Trade is quoted in Maclean's magazine: "Most of the auto parts work in Canada is not

March 14, 1991
Oral Questions
highly skilled. That kind of work will be done in Mexico or it will be done somewhere like Mexico, other than in Canada".
Is this why the minister is rushing hell-bent into a free trade agreement with Mexico?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to discover that the hon. gentleman reads Maclean's magazine.
If he looked at the transcript of the reporter who conducted the interview he would see exactly what I said. I said that with respect to low value-added and less skilled work in the auto parts industry, that is a matter where we cannot stop competition from lower wage countries such as Mexico and many others being extremely effective.
We are interested in the higher value added, skilled end of the industry, and there Canada can compete just as the auto parts manufacturers say they can. There we will compete and there we will be very competitive under free trade. With free trade we are globally competitive, and there is nothing to be afraid of if you have any faith in the auto parts industry or in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, auto parts manufacturers of Canada do not agree with the minister. According to their letter, the auto parts industry is in the vanguard of high technology in Canada's manufacturing base in terms of automation, robotics, and other technologies. They say: "Your comments are unacceptable to us. Your comments are criticizing the technological skills base of not only the 75,000 auto parts manufacturers in Canada, but the 300,000 other related workers in related industries".
Will the minister take back his statements? Will he start fighting on behalf of Canadian jobs and workers rather than just dismissing them with the stroke of a pen?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these are the gravest accusations since Emile Zola.
Members of the auto parts industry just wrote me a letter. Apparently they sent the hon. gentleman a copy, because they read the same article as the hon. member and have drawn the same wrong conclusion as the hon. member. I never said what they say I have said, or you
said I said. I never said it, as I just explained a few minutes ago.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday the United States President appeared to dump cold water on the idea of a global summit on arms sales, an idea which had support on all sides of the House.
The United States and other countries in fact are already lining up to sell arms to the Middle East, despite the admonition of the Prime Minister to the contrary.
Can the Prime Minister report to the House on this aspect of his talks yesterday with President Bush? Is the global summit dead? Are there alternatives that the government would have in mind if in fact the idea is a goner?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that President Bush, were he here, would want me to correct the misstatement in the prefatory remarks of my hon. friend. He did not throw cold water on it.
As the minister of trade suggests, it is important to read the transcript. Here is what he said. "I am not sure exactly what the proper structure is for this, but clearly that idea"-namely the one that Canada put forward-"may, indeed, have some merit".
Pursuant to this, we began the process of examining it last night. The Secretary of State for External Affairs met with eight heads of government, I believe, throughout the region in the last number of days. All of them believe that it had some merit. The President is going to examine it today with President Mitterrand and over the weekend with Prime Minister Major, and slowly but surely, hopefully the idea will advance.
We think it is a good one. We put it forward vigorously on behalf of Canada. I indicated the contradiction, of the five permanent members of the Security Council persist in large, vast arms sales to the countries in the region, and then are perplexed by the fact that some members in the region decide to use them to wage war against innocent members. This does not make any sense. We
March 14, 1991

believe the Canadian position is a consistent and a reasonably thoughtful one. After a period of reflection, others will subscribe to it.

speechtext: The hon. member for Richelieu now has the floor. One question only, please.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should advise the House that I have a question of privilege from the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Labour, when asked what the government would do about the 14.3 per cent unemployment rate in Montreal, the highest municipal rate in Canada, did not answer the question, but said, and I quote from page 18397 of Hansard:
Business of the House
-we should make allowances for the hon. member for Saint-Laurent-Cartierville who may not have all the facts, but we cannot make the same allowances for the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace who has been sitting in this House as a Liberal member for 25 years.
He went on to say:
Before 1984-during the last 17 or 18 years the Liberals were in
power in this country, Montreal lost not 100, not 200, but 4,000 jobs.
Between the election of a Liberal government in 1965 and the election of a Conservative government in 1979, a period of 14 years, when I was a member of this House and a member of the government, the average rate of unemployment in Canada was 6 per cent, and in Montreal it was 6.7 per cent, and thousands of new jobs were created, a record never matched by this Conservative government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have looked at the exchange in Hansard. I also have examined carefully the notice which was given according to the rules by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace.
