speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose the weekly question to the government House leader. Could he indicate to the House what the business will be for tomorrow, Monday, Tbesday and the rest of the next week?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to formally designate tomorrow as an allotted day for supply.
It would be my intention at this time to designate next Monday as an allotted day as well. I would like to keep open the possibility of discussions with respect to that date, but that is the intention at this time.
On Tuesday, March 19, I plan to call report stage and third reading of Bill C-97, the borrowing bill and, hopefully, complete both stages by the end of that day.

March 14, 1991
Business of the House
I would like to carry on with the discussions between House leaders to see how we might most effectively and efficiently decide on business for the remainder of next week.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order with my hon. friend the government House leader, I wonder if I could seek clarification on the point regarding the eventual introduction of legislation to impose the tax on cigarette products.
When the budget was tabled on February 26 a ways and means motion was also tabled. We have yet to have the final two days of the budget debate. My hon. friend will know that until those two days of debate take place the Standing Orders make it impossible to introduce the ways and means motion which would then give legal authority to collect the tax on cigarettes.
I suppose one could always make the case that at the moment the government lacks the legal authority for the collection of this tax but I would like to say that since it has already been introduced perhaps we should talk about ways and means of facilitating the passage of this bill.
Could my friend give some indication as to whether or not he plans to bring in that legislation soon.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows in fact there are ample legal precedents to collect the tax at the time indicated in the ways and means motion during a budget. I know that from experience having, while in opposition, challenged the government's right to collect taxes on the basis of a ways and means motion. It wasted a lot of time and money on legal opinions which confirmed that, in fact, all that is necessary is that at some point legislation be brought forward to change the law. That needs to be preceded by adoption of the ways and means motion.
The hon. member is right, it can be done after the approval of the general motion attached to a budget. Of course should events intervene such as prorogation, none of that applies and it becomes academic.
It is in regard to discussions such as that that I look forward to discussing our plans for future deliberations in this House with my hon. friend and the House leader of the Liberal Party.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps my hon. friend has misunderstood the point I was making.
Technically, I agree with him based on terms of past precedents, but retailers have been collecting this tax and consumers have been paying the tax in good faith based on the announcement of the Minister of Finance during the budget presentation. Yet the government does not seem to be delivering in good faith, in terms of their initiative, legislation that would clearly authorize the collection of this tax.
I am simply saying to my friend that I look forward to facilitating this discussion so that we can react in the same good faith that consumers and retailers are showing.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point I was making is that it is not merely good faith. I do not think there is an option available to consumers in that regard.
I appreciate the offer of the hon. member to facilitate the passage of the budget bills. There will be that budget bill, plus one or two others coming from the budget and I look forward to our discussions to find a way in which we can facilitate the passage of those bills as early as possible.
My seatmate, the Minister of Finance, informed me yesterday that the draughtsmen are beavering away and in short order should have those bills available for first reading.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the government House leader. He is talking about some delays as a result of the government draughtspersons not being ready to introduce legislation. However, prior to the House sitting in mid-February, the Minister of Finance had draft legislation on the northern tax benefits. He circulated not only the legislation, but he also circulated the regulations. However, that legislation which he circulated across this country has never been introduced into the House of Commons.
Since the Minister of Finance felt capable of circulating this legislation far and wide, could the government House leader indicate why Canadians who are now able, as a result of the government's announcement last December, to claim for at least a partial northern tax benefit; why they have to sit and wait for their rebates and any money that is owing to them by the federal government, and why they have to wait and wait when this legislation was presumably written, since the government can circulate it.
March 14, 1991

This is the third week in a row that I have asked this question. Why has the government not introduced that legislation into the House?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member is right; this is the third week in a row. And for the third week in a row let me say that just as soon as his party is ready to discuss and co-operate in getting legislation passed, we are ready to proceed.
It is absurd for the hon. member to imply that this program, which was brought forward by this government, which we recognize as beneficial to northerners-we did it deliberately-that somehow we would be wanting to drag our feet on it. That is absurd. Of course we want to proceed with it.
We have some other matters. We are running into time difficulties. I am looking forward to profitable discussions, which I hope we can have soon, to find a way to expedite the treatment of that bill and others.

Again, to remind the government House leader, there has not been a request from the government to the opposition parties to move on the northern tax benefit legislation. It is awfully hard for us to respond if we are not asked to.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Berger (p. 18439).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa West will have 10 minutes plus 5 minutes questions and comments.

It is my pleasure to rise today and speak on this motion, bringing to the attention of Canadians promises of the Prime Minister with respect to research and technology in Canada, and the abysmal failure on the delivery of those promises.
I would like to begin by talking about the fundamental importance I see of investment in science research and technology, particularly at this stage in our history.
Supply
Canada went through a period where exploration was extremely important to our development as a nation. At that time the new frontiers were the frontiers of geography, climate and distance. We mastered those and we conquered those and we created a country. Now we are heading into the 21st century and the frontiers are no longer physical frontiers but the frontiers of the human mind and spirit.
That is what science is all about; it is launching off on those marvellous explorations, not knowing necessarily exactly where and when we will get to where we are going, but knowing that inevitably tremendous and new discoveries will be made.
It is in those discoveries by the human mind of the way the world functions that the prosperity of any nation rests in the coming century.
The failure of the government to recognize this has done irreparable damage to the Canadian economy, which is only now beginning to be felt and which will become even deeper and more prolonged as time goes on.
I want to go to the promises made by the Prime Minister in 1984 when he was still leader of the opposition. He promised Canadians a spending commitment on research and development during the first mandate of his government. He promised lower interest rates. He promised the development of job training and the development of trade.
I will come specifically to the abysmal failure to keep the commitment on research and development in a moment. I do want to talk about lower interest rates. We know that one of the reasons we have the huge debt and deficit we have now is because of the high interest rate policy of this government. We know that rather than the development of job training we have had major slashes to funding for job training and development. We have had massive cuts to post-secondary education.
He promised the development of trade. In the days since that promise, Canada's trade surplus has dropped dramatically. Our trade in high technology is in a deficit position. We have a competitiveness with our major trading partners that is less than it was 10 years ago. We now rank last, or second last, in eight of the ten economic indicators in science and technology used by the OECD. R and D spending has declined.

March 14, 1991

Our competitiveness has been reduced, not increased. The only thing we are trading and exporting more than we were before is jobs.
The government has failed to deal with poverty, which is a major impediment to education and to the improvement of the talent and the use of talent of our young people.
Going specifically to research and development, I want to go over what is a rather sorry history of this government and a total abandonment of the Prime Minister's promise. It has been a reversal of the progress towards improved research and development in this country. It goes well beyond simply the fact that funding to research and development has been decimated. It goes well beyond blaming the private sector for not doing the job that is the job of the public sector, namely, protecting the national interests and protecting the national wealth of knowledge and the foundation of progress in technology.
As the minister himself has said, "Our competitors increase their research and development, when times get bad. They know the answer is to look for new ways." Why is the minister out there admonishing the private sector to increase R and D when times are bad, while he stands in this House and says we have to cut research and development; that we have to cut science when times are bad? The same lesson applies for the government that applies for our competitors, the same lesson the minister wants to deliver to the private sector.
The National Research Council, a hallmark, the envy of the international community in progress in science and innovation, has been subject to savage attacks repeatedly over seven years. We have had a downsizing program in the public service that has left scientists spending half their time doing their own clerical work. Who, with a grain of economic common sense, would save money on a $25,000 a year clerical position, to have a scientist earning $65,000 a year do clerical work half the time?
We have companies specializing in research being sold off or bought off by foreign interests, further reducing the ability of the private sector to build the intellectual wealth of this country. We have the loss of Connaught Labs. We have the loss of Lumonics. We have young people refusing to go into science. Only 20 per cent of admissions to university are in science. They see no future, because this government has said there is no future. Twenty per cent of the National Research Council now has either been shoved out the door or bought off.
The minister had the temerity today to talk about women in science. Increasing the number of women in science is a useful and important strategy because we know that we have fewer young people coming into the labour market at all levels and that we are going to face a severe shortage at all levels of the labour market. One way of overcoming the shortages is to ensure that women, as well as men, develop their talents to the fullest.
What does this government do to women scientists? Less than 25 per cent of its professional scientists are women, and most of them are in short-term positions. They are renewed and renewed, but they are never hired as full-time permanent employees. Very few women scientists ever retire from the Government of Canada because they get fed up and they leave.
All the words the minister may have about attracting women into science are not going to work until women see career opportunities in government science, and career opportunities in the private sector in science. Until then we will be wasting our money.
We are losing opportunities to be world leaders in environmental technology. The NSERC told us years ago that this was a major trading and growth opportunity for the Government of Canada, and yet this government-in the midst of the global warming crisis-has decimated, literally, from $500 million to $50 million what we spend on alternative energy and on conservation of fossil fuels.
Instead of pursuing all options to show the world new ways of using energy and of prospering without destroying the very air we breathe, the government has cut out the energy sector at the environmental secretariat and it has cut the energy division at the National Research Council. Now it is scrambling to restore some symbolic but insignificant remnant of both of those important divisions that existed and were thriving just seven short years ago.
I could list a litany of cuts to environmentally important programs. While the world is desperate for good environmental technology to preserve the very ability of this planet to survive and thrive, not only are we failing to perform a useful function in the world through the development of our environmental technology but we
March 14, 1991

are missing a major economic opportunity to make Canada a world leader in many environmental areas.
The government talks about the deficit and the debt, and I like to talk about the human deficit.
We would not have a debt and a deficit if we did not have 10.5 per cent of our people unemployed. If we had people earning and contributing to the economy instead of requiring support from the economy, if we had people with purchasing power in their pockets creating jobs for other Canadians by the purchase of goods and services, we would have a healthy economy. If we were investing in the education of our young people, if we were investing in the kind of science and technology that gives us new opportunities in the world and gives us an opportunity to reverse our deficit in the export of high technology, then we might start to work our way out of this difficult economic situation.
But that is not the way of this government. The way of this government is to destroy, to cut, to squander opportunities. That is what has been happening in science and technology, in research and development in this country now for seven years.

speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly pleased to participate in the debate this afternoon.
I will not be as fiery as my colleague, the minister from Newfoundland, but I will do my bit to perhaps antagonize some of my colleagues opposite as they are trying to do to us.
When a member comes into the House, he usually brings with him several interests or hobby horses that he
may have. When I came into the House back in 1974, 16 years or more ago, I was like that as well. One of those interests was science and technology, and research and development. Mr. Speaker, you will not be offended if I suggest that you, Sir, along with two others in the House this afternoon are old-timers here. You, Sir, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace will remember, but other members will not recall the policy of the then Liberal government regarding science and technology. When I listened to the member for Ottawa West try to criticize us, it was unfortunate that she had not taken a little time to read about the history of science and technology as it relates to the House of Commons and the various governments over the last couple of decades.
The truth of the matter is that roughly 15 or 16 years ago I sat in the House here and listened to the then minister of science and technology. I believe he was at that time the member for Westmount. He indicated to the House when we were challenging him from the opposition, that really we did not have to spend much money on science and technology. That was a waste of money. We should be just buying our research and development and our science and technology from neighbouring countries like the U.S.A. or U.K. or Germany, where they were doing that. They would do it for us and we could acquire it from them. That was the official position of the Liberal Party at that time.
The other interesting thing, to take you a little bit back in history, that you will recall yourself, Mr. Speaker, is that at that time if you were interested in science and technology and you wanted to question the minister, the estimates did not come before any standing committee on that at all. Where they went at that time was to a committee known as the committee on miscellaneous estimates. That was a waste paper basket of all sorts of little things.
That was the priority that the government at that time gave to science and technology. Estimates at that time were referred to the miscellaneous estimates committee. There were three or four of us in the opposition who thought that was not good enough for science and technology, that we should be doing better. We tried to prevail upon the government of that day to create a
March 14, 1991

standing committee, but no such luck. Nothing happened.
It was not, Sir, and I will remind you, until 1984 when our present government came into power that a standing committee on science and technology was established. The Conservative Party recognized the importance of science and technology. We now have that committee. I believe you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the original chairman, if my memory is correct, was Dr. Bill Tupper, who sat here from one of the ridings in the Ottawa region, a very renowned scientist in Canada and a lecturer at the university. He sat as the first chairman of that committee and I had the privilege of sitting on that committee.
I think it is imperative that we bring to mind the past history before we start criticizing too much the present government. As the Minister for International Trade has pointed out, there are very trying circumstances at the present time and in spite of those circumstances, we are managing to increase our contribution to science and technology, albeit we would like to do it a little bit faster.
There are a number of areas that one could talk about in a debate such as this, but I would like to put a little emphasis on the area of the Canada Scholarship Program. The motion we have before us today in the House does not even mention perhaps the most crucial aspect of research and development and science and technology, and that is people. I think we have to remind ourselves that when we speak of research and development, and we speak of science and technology, we cannot afford to lose sight of that vital ingredient in the equation. That ingredient is indeed people. We are talking here of the highly qualified men and women who need to drive this remarkable technological revolution forward from the present time.
There have been recent studies done, including those done by our own Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council which have shown that Canada faces a crisis situation with a shortage of highly qualified scientists and engineers. Here we are talking about people. The proportion of students who now enter science and engineering has remained relatively constant at about 20 per cent over this past decade. I think that was alluded to by the member for Ottawa West. It has not grown actually in response to the needs that are out there at the present time.

Though we may be only second to the United States in the number of post-secondary school graduates as a percentage of the work force, we do have a low rate of scientists and engineers. That is the problem that we as a government have identified over the last six years and are now trying to correct.
Moreover, the Economic Council of Canada has predicted that the technological content of all jobs, not just the scientists and engineering jobs but all jobs, are going to increase. The requirement is going to increase down the road and we will, therefore, need an even higher proportion of scientists and engineers in the work force than we have had over the past decade.
There is no doubt that we are committed to valuing scientific and engineering achievements and to providing appropriate recognition and rewards for contributions in these fields in order to attract students into it. It is this kind of remuneration and reward system for the science and engineering professions which has never been on par with some of the other professions such as the legal and medical professions. As a society, we have to take some blame for that.
It seems to us that the key, if we are going to reach our young people, these young women and men in our elementary schools and high schools, we have to make it attractive for them. We need to make them aware of how science and technology affect their lives. We need to get them excited about science and technology and we need to encourage them to pursue the wide range of career opportunities that exist in these fields.
I am proud to say that our government is playing a leadership role in this regard and we have done so under a number of initiatives, an important one of which is the Canada Scholarship Program, which is an excellent example of one of those initiatives.
When the Prime Minister launched the Canada Scholarship Program some three years ago, he spoke then about the bright minds and about the commitment of our government to ensuring that the talents of these young Canadians would be appropriately recognized and rewarded.
This program is now entering its third year. It represents an $80 million investment, which is a significant amount of money, over five years by the Government of Canada in its continuing commitment to excellence in scientific and engineering education.

March 14, 1991

Based on outstanding academic performance, first-year students at the post-secondary level enrolled in science and engineering related disciplines are eligible to receive $2,000 a year for up to four years for a total of $8,000. We have now, over the course of the last three years, been able to help some 6,200 scholars, who are benefiting from what is offered under this Canada Scholarship Program.
One of the interesting things is that we are also getting industry involved. That has been alluded to by my friend from Ottawa West. For example, the Ballard Power Systems of Victoria and the Corel Systems here in Ottawa, among others, are funding the Canada Scholars Frontrunners Project which will be of some significance. The DuPont Company-Governor General's Canada Scholarship in Environmental Engineering also has to be recognized. Canadian Marconi is supporting the creation of Canada Scholars Mentor Clubs. The Nova Corporation of Alberta is funding special scholarship awards for Canada scholars.
Other corporations such as GE Canada, SCIEX Inc., MDS Health Group, DuPont Canada, Merck Frosst Canada, Rio Algom Ltd., Pan Canadian Petroleum and Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting are all involved from the private sector in trying to help out in this area.
But without a doubt, the success of these programs depends on the scholars themselves and their motivation and the ability that we have to encourage them to get into this field of endeavour, which is so crucial for our future competitive position in world affairs.
It is this Canada Scholarship Program which now stands as a glowing example of our government's ongoing effort to foster excellence in science and engineering education here in Canada. Combined with initiatives such as the science and technology public awareness campaign and the National Networks of Centres of Excellence, it represents an unprecedented federal commitment.
I conclude by suggesting that it is a commitment that I am indeed proud to talk about this afternoon and it is a commitment that will ensure a competitive Canada and a prosperous and rewarding future for our young people.

I compliment my colleague and friend on that very fine talk on research and development, but there are some questions that we have on this side of the House that cause us a great deal of concern and seemed not to be properly addressed in this budget with the expenditures of money.
Let me just relate some facts. I am so glad that the Minister for International Trade has decided to stay with us because I think these facts reflect something about what he had to say to our previous speaker.
It is a little known fact in Canada today that the largest single industry is forestry. It is larger than either the automobile or the petroleum industries in Canada. Forestry in Canada employs over 8 per cent of our Canadian labour force and it supports over 900,000 forestry manufacturing and service jobs.
One out of every seven manufacturing dollars in Canada is related directly to this industry, and it contributes more than $17 billion to Canada's net trade balance. Forestry accounts for close to $2.5 billion in trade within our country alone.
Government policy does not reflect the importance of this industry to over 300 communities in Canada that are dependent solely on the forestry industry for their sole survival. It does not reflect this industry's contribution to the national economy and its treatment toward more than 30 single industry towns in northern Ontario alone, the area I represent.
With that background, let us consider the remarks the Minister for International Trade made just a few moments ago and discuss what the forestry industry is doing for our country and the lack of public expenditures to this most vital of all industries. Looking at the forecasts for 1990 and 1991 in the budgetary expenditures, $53 million was spent last year in that area. In the estimates for 1991 and 1992 that has been reduced by almost $20 million. It is now down to $33,900,000, a drop of $20 million which certainly does not reflect the tremendous importance of this vital industry in Canada.
Perhaps I may just address the comments made by the Minister for International Trade. One of the things that can be done-and it is so vital and does not cost our
March 14, 1991

country one penny-is the elimination of the 15 per cent export tax that was placed in 1986 on the softwood lumber exports to the United States.
We have been asking the government to remove that tax because of its unfairness to the people in small communities in this country. It is not going to cost Canadians anything. It is just a simple determination that the 15 per cent tax on the softwood lumber industry in Canada, particularly in British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario, has imposed personal anguish and suffering on people who are involved in these single industry towns. It can be eliminated by eliminating that unfair tax and letting these people in these industries in these towns compete with the Americans on a level playing field.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to this, although it is a little bit off the topic of science and technology and research and development. I have a bit of a personal interest in the subject area of forestry, having worked one summer in the area of Thunder Bay-Nipigon. Having cut pulp up there, I have quite a bit of sympathy for the work that goes on in that area.
I am also concerned about science and technology in the forestry area. There is no doubt that we need to spend money there. I had occasion to meet with a Russian scientist a little over a year ago in Moscow and subsequently here in Canada, who is working very diligently on a scheme that will eliminate waste products that currently come from our forest product manufacturing plants here in Canada, whereby pulp would be produced without any waste product of significance at all. I agree that there is room for further study.
As to the tax on softwood lumber, I suppose the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon should probably speak with his colleagues from New Brunswick. He might get a little different slant on that tax from them. I appreciate the needs of our lumbering industry and the forest industry.
I am pleased to say also, from the point of view of the private sector and as one who is interested in disabled and handicapped people, that members of the union in the forestry sector and the management of those same plants are now working together to try to help injured workers and reintegrate them into the work place.

Those workers and those management people in the forestry sector deserve credit for the work they are doing, which I think is of great importance to Canada.
I share the member's concern about this tax problem. It is a difficult one. But the Prime Minister, as we heard this afternoon, is addressing that problem with the President of the U.S.A. himself. I hope we will see a resolution that will satisfy all sides.

Mr. Speaker, like many of my colleagues who are participating in this debate this afternoon, I welcome the opportunity to review the opposition motion and its suggestion that the Prime Minister failed in honouring a commitment to double Canada's spending commitment to research and development.
Could you repeat that?

If the members opposite have a hard time hearing, maybe they should plug in their hearing aids. I think I have made myself fairly clear.
Let us examine the statement. Perhaps the exact doubling of these expenditures, which they have a complaint about, is the problem. We have heard this afternoon from my colleagues who just spoke, the member for Oxford and the Minister for International Trade, and in fact the Prime Minister. I can assure all members in this House that from the perspective of one area of Canada, the one I come from, our Prime Minister is light-years ahead of anything that has ever previously been accomplished by any leader of this country, probably Conservatives included, in focusing on science and technology.
Let us recognize that fact. Our Prime Minister made this one of his projects. He made some commitments for funding. Although the argument has been made that they have not been totally achieved according to what he said in 1984 or previously, I think the example that he has

given and the leadership role he has played have focused attention on this particular area of concern to Canadians.
I do not think anyone in the seats opposite can argue otherwise. They may sit and laugh, but what other Prime Minister can they mention who has taken such a tremendous initiative and a leadership role? I do not think they should sit in their places and laugh at it. Certainly Mr. Trudeau didn't, certainly the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra didn't, certainly Mr. Pearson didn't, and quite possibly they might say that for nine months neither did the right hon. member for Yellowhead.
I do not think using this particular style of discussing the issues of science and technology will really indicate that we have not gone far enough. I suppose members on this side will suggest that maybe we should have gone further. But this party, under its leadership, has not gone out in any reckless way to throw money at projects, because we have always used that as a consideration point.
I would like to say, if I may, that if we look at some of the things that have happened as a result of the leadership of our Prime Minister, we see that a lot of things have happened to our young people as well. My children in school have science fairs, and I really believe that a focus on science and technology is occurring in the schools. They have taken it upon themselves from the educators and a direction, not just from the Prime Minister but from a lot of the scientific leaders in our country, to focus attention on the importance of the changes in technology and bring it to the attention of the young people.
As I said, my children in school do a lot of things differently than when I went to school some 20 years ago. Science fairs are really an "in" thing, and I think my colleagues opposite will probably have noticed that change as well.
That is drawing attention, maybe not with big dollars, to create an awareness in young people so that when they reach maturity and have completed their scholastic activities, they will see the importance of science, change, and technology and why we should continue this research, this important part of the development of our country.
As a farmer, although not active in recent years but in former years, I know that the importance of technological change in agriculture is fantastic and phenomenal. Canadian companies and researchers in universities are very often in the forefront of the technological change we are talking about.
Let us look at the production of wheat. We may argue and the opposition may argue that the farmers are not getting enough money for that wheat. Through the technology and science that has been applied to this very important part of agriculture, not just within Canada but around the world, scientists in Canada are producing wheat that doubles production compared to what we had in the late 1930s and 1940s. Consequently we are helping to feed the world.
That research has not stopped. It continues even in the oilseed crops. Canada is a leader in the production of a canola meal that has fewer impurities than in the beginning. This crop, through Canadian science and technology, has been developed into what is almost a perfect crop.
What about hog research?

My colleague suggested that I talk a bit about hog research. He is absolutely right. The technology in the production of better quality pork has made Canada's pork among the very best in the world. This is a result of research done at universities. A lot of people do not realize that we are now producing a hog that grows faster with greater feed conversion and less fat. This kind of research continues because the average consumer and everyone in this room do not like to eat as much fat. Because of such things as cholesterol it is not the healthy food we once thought it was.
It is also important to the farmer to produce a hog at less cost; in other words, feed efficiency, the ability to convert roughage and feed into meat, into protein. There have been tremendous steps forward in agricultural research. This is continuing, and I think we owe a great debt to the many scientists who are working on such projects.
Cuts to projects in terms of funding concern those on all sides of the House, but we have to balance that with what is available and what are the priorities. These are difficult decisions. No one will deny that it is not an easy decision to cut a project on which scientists in this countiy are doing research. It would not matter if members opposite were sitting on this side of the House.
March 14, 1991

From time to time those decisions have to be made and I have experienced that.
It is important to look at the technological change and transfer that is going on. I think the fact that the Prime Minister has focused so much of his personal time on this particular endeavour is, consider him as you may, the most positive thing that a Prime Minister has done in this country for years.
Science is important to us and we should look at other countries. The best thing to do is compare. My colleagues opposite see what has happened since the war in the great countries of Japan and Germany, as well as in some other countries such as that great giant to the south of us, the United States. I was an international exporter as well as a fanner before coming here and know that these countries consider Canada to be doing tremendous advance work in many fields important to Canadians and to Canadian business people.
We should consider those few facts alone and consider where we ought to be going. Sometimes we look at a country like Germany and say: "How is it able to come out with this fantastic Mercedes Benz?" Lately we have seen the latest research and technology going into the Lexus car from Japan and the energies private companies have used, not the government so much but private companies.
I believe that in our efforts to continue that scientific research and technology sometimes we ought to give more assistance to the companies as maybe a tax writeoff, which I am sure they get anyway, if their research is going to lead to better productivity, more efficient products and ones that Canadians can help work to build and manufacture, where we shine.
We do shine in agriculture, but I think we also shine now as a country in bringing this awareness to our youth. The young people are doing so much more. I think that whole attitude will bring them into the sciences at university. It is a future they can depend on because we need a lot more scientists. I am happy to say that one of my sons is looking into computer science. I am very proud of him because he sees a future in it. There is lots of opportunity if we keep letting our young people know that they exist and that we support them.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Portage-Interlake for his interesting presentation. I took into perspective what he said about the reputation he alluded

to that Canada has in agricultural research. I would accept that because I do recognize his expertise in the field of agriculture. I had some personal experience on the trip that we had together. Certainly as somebody who has knowledge of the fishing industry, I was impressed with his knowledge.
Probably where we stand on this issue could depend on where we sit with respect to how selective we want to be.
I will accept that Canada has leadership in technology, research and development in the agriculture field, and I would like to relate that to the fishing industry. I would like to bring to the member's attention that Canada is the world's largest leading fish exporter. I was at a conference about three years ago where it was suggested that Canada's fisheries, from the scientific viewpoint and scientific research, are now where Europe's were 15 years ago.
I really have to reflect on what the fishing industry could be doing without this technological lag, what the predictions would be with respect to the northern cod and other areas of scientific information, knowledge and indeed research that I would have to recognize have been addressed to a certain extent in the Atlantic Fish Adjustment Program.
The fact remains that certainly we are the largest exporter in the world and I think a leading authority because of our geography, our three coasts and our continental shelf. Areas of excellence and centres of excellence could well be developed.
I am going to speak in a few moments on this subject. I do not want to take up any more of the hon. member's time. I would like him to reflect that there are certain areas we really could be improving in and they are key areas as far as I am concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I acknowledge my hon. colleague from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception and I have had a small association in looking at different parts of the country once on a short visit. I cherished the exchange of views that he and I had.
I can only agree with his statement that there are many areas of importance with respect to the advancements of technology. I will just give him a brief example of what he has said with regard to fish. Believe me, I represent an area, for some who do not know, that has 1,200 commercial fishermen producing something like $40 million worth of fish products in the heart of this

country, on the prairies of Canada, through the Freshwater Fish Corporation.
While I was campaigning in Gimli in 1984,1 was met by a street vendor who was selling some crab sticks. These were made in Japan. They were not made of crabmeat, but they tasted so much litre crabmeat that the chap was doing very well.
I thought to myself, in the middle of fishing country and in the heart of the continent, here we have a Japanese technology that has produced a very palatable product and something that I would buy. I had the pleasure of making a submission to that panel in September 1989. The panel's report called Protecting our Waters is a devastating critique of Canada's current ability to prevent or respond effectively to oil spills. I will quote from the report:
The capacity to respond effectively to a spill of any significant magnitude does not presently exist anywhere in Canada.

A major research and development effort is urgently needed to develop more effective spill clean-up equipment and technology because what is now available is essentially primitive and largely ineffectual.
This panel made over 100 recommendations and costed them at approximately $1.5 billion over a 10-year period. It suggested that $800 million to $1 billion could be raised through a $2 per tonne levy on all oil products transported in Canadian waters.
It recommended that part of these funds could go towards enhancing Canada's spill response capability. This would be done by upgrading government co-ordinated and government funded research and development into spill response technologies and by supporting the establishment of a major industry operated spill response co-operative in all high risk areas in Canada.
The panel's interim report in September 1989 noted that both government and industry have significantly reduced their funding of oil spill response R and D over the past decade. According to the panel, there is a glaring need for more extensive research into the longterm effects of oil and chemical pollution.

Environment Canada co-ordinated a multimillion dollar government-industry research program, but Environment Canada's funding for oil spill research and development has declined substantially since the 1970s. Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in the debate this afternoon on the Liberal motion in front of us.
Much has been said today on the need for further research and development in Canada. When we do away with all the rhetoric that we have heard today, there is fundamental agreement among all political parties in this House that as a nation we must strengthen our ability to do research which is both basic and applied and to use the findings of our research in developing new services and new products.
If we are to survive in the type of competitive world we live in, we have to recognize and acknowledge that it is a world of very rapid changes where traditional trading patterns are being changed all the time, and that the only way to survive is through smart technology, smart trade strategies, smart economic strategies.
It requires a nation with a high degree of research and development, a high capacity for processing information, a capacity for being able to use what it has learned to implement and practise that knowledge.
It is not enough for us to do R and D and then not use that knowledge. It is not enough for us to have all the information at our fingertips, stored in computer data bases, and not be able to use that data to affect our behaviour or our trading strategies, et cetera, that would allow us a competitive edge in the world today.
We could talk a bit about the records of the present government. I would tend to think that most hon. members would agree that the Minister for Science, if he was not on public display but more in the privacy of a private conversation, over a beer or over a lunch, would admit that the record is not as great as he would have hoped it to be.
I am sure that some of our Liberal colleagues in a private situation would admit that programs like the scientific research fund, which Mr. Lalonde introduced in the dying days of the Liberal regime, was indeed a
tremendous waste of public money and a waste of money that could and should have gone to proper research. I am sure my Liberal colleagues, in the privacy of a private conversation, would admit that more should and could have been done when they were in government those long decades.
However, it is not enough to acknowledge the need to do more in private. What becomes important is for us as an entity, as a Parliament together, to be able to affect the thinking and the priorities of the government so that it begins to recognize, not in a private way but in a public way, in a way that results in action, that if we are to survive as a trading nation we must spend more on research and development.
We have to recognize that an erosion is occurring in Canada, and let not political gamesmanship, pointing blame or defending oneself, and the huffing and the political puffing hide the fact that our universities are deteriorating.
A year ago I had a tour of some of our universities across this country: some in Alberta, some in Saskatchewan, some in Manitoba, some in Ontario. I talked to faculty and to students. In one university, students told me they have exactly 15 minutes to spend with a book because there is such a line-up behind them waiting for the same source book. Our libraries are badly underfunded and cannot keep up with the latest journals, magazines and books that are being published. Our Canadian students do not have access to the latest in their particular field of expertise.
At another university, I was told about their lab equipment that had not been properly replaced and upgraded since the early 1970s when there was a spurt of spending in R and D and in universities. Those students are using lab equipment that is at least a decade and in some cases two decades old. Those students do not have an opportunity to deal with the latest technology.
I hear stories of the difficulty of getting entrance into university, that more universities are having to set higher requirements. Just recently I noticed that the university in my home city, the University of Regina, is talking about establishing quotas in its different faculties. It does not have the space and the faculty to meet the demand that is out there for higher education.

Yet, the demographics will tell us that we are going to have a shortage in this country of trained people. We are going to need scientists, engineers and teachers. We are going to be having a shortage at some point in the future.
Elistorically we have made up the deficit by importing graduates out of Italy, Holland, Germany, England and the other European countries, but that is not possible any more. We cannot expect waves of scientists and trained people from Europe to come and fill the need that exists in Canada.
We see the sad situation arising. Here we have young Canadian men and women desiring post-secondary education. We know that down the road they are going to be needed, that we are going to have a shortage. Yet, somehow or other we are not able to bring together these two central facts and do something about it.
Recently I have had an opportunity to see some of the scientific sectors that exist in other countries. The one that impressed me the most was the one I saw in Taiwan where there is a tremendous combination of resources. There is a co-ordination of resources between the private and the public sectors not just in terms of dealing with the research and development of R and, D but also the marketing of it.
Is it not about time that we in North America began to realize that our traditional economic model, which is essentially one of competition, an adversarial model, is not going to make do in the 21st century? When we see economic giants such as Japan and Germany, we begin to realize that they have a different economic and social structure. They have one in which the private and public sectors co-operate very closely. Nowhere is that co-operation closer than in the area of research and development.
The public sector and the private sectors sit down and work together to target certain areas. Certain tax concessions, the raising of capital, and the focusing of the country's resources, whether through the public or private sectors, are brought together to bear on the goal.
We have seen both Germany and Japan become technological leaders. They have taken certain fields and developed expertise in those fields. Then with the co-ordination of the public and the private sector, and I should include the trade unions as well, they worked
Supply
together to create for themselves high-tech industries that create employment, good employment with high paying jobs, and wealth for the country and that help the general good of the nation.
That is a model I think we have to seriously start looking at. The adversarial model between the public and the private sector and between different industries and between labour and business is one that in essence is self-destructive. Nowhere is it more self-destructive than in the area of research and development. A new attitude and new thinking are needed if we are to survive economically.
When we contrast the state of our universities and the state of R and D in this country with the state of the universities and R and D in countries like Japan and Germany, I think it becomes obvious and very plain what the difference is and why some succeed and others do not.
We also have a basic structural problem in this country when it comes to R and D. That was enunciated many years ago by the Lamontagne committee report on research and development. What it found was that-and I believe that paper was done in the early seventies- compared to other nations in the world our public expenditure on R and D at that time was a little bit more than what public expenditure was in most of the industrialized countries in the world. What they found significant was that the private R and D done was way below what was normally done in the other OECD countries. When they broke that down a little further, they discovered that Canadian owned businesses did quite well when it came to R and D and that it was the multinational firms that did so poorly when it came to R and D.
In some ways that is logical. It should not surprise us at all that a multinational firm generally does its research and development in its own country. Our economic structure is such that so much of our industry is foreign owned by multinationals which do little research in this country. That is what the Lamontagne committee report pin-pointed as a structural problem that we had.
When I heard earlier today some of the remarks from our Liberal colleagues about R and D, attacking the NDP for being anti-business, I chuckled. Many of the things that my colleague, our critic for science and research, was saying were things to be found in the

March 14, 1991
Supply
Lamontagne report. The Lamontagne report of course was a Liberal report, but then perhaps Mr. Lamontagne was of the old school, of the old Liberal school of Walter Gordon and Mr. Kierans, the old school that died in the sixties, the old school that believed in Canadian economic nationalism.
It is no wonder that we see the evolution of the Liberal Party coming around to the point where when we say things that are not unusual, in fact things that Liberals like Eric Kierans and Mr. Lamontagne around that time were saying now are considered by the Liberals in the House as being anti-business, socialist, sloganeering, totally impractical and off the wall. So be it.
If we are going to deal seriously with the question of R and D in this country we have to be able to mobilize industry, the public sector and labour. I suggest that it is harder to mobilize industry when it is a multinational industry. Canadian industry which has some roots and loyalty to this country can work together in a common strategy to do the research and then do the development and the marketing. That becomes, of course, insurmountable when we are dealing with an economy where vast chunks of it is owned by foreigners through foreign multinationals.
I could stand here and recite statistics concerning the record of the present government. I think they have already been put on the record. I do not want to get into this game because really what we are doing on the floor of the House of Commons is posturing.
As I suggested before, I am certain that in a private discussion, my hon. friend from the Liberal Party and my friend the Minister for Science, sitting privately together without the television sets and the microphones and so forth, we would find, I am sure, 99 per cent agreement. It is a pity that basic agreement cannot be brought out here into the public forum, that we cannot take that agreement and really create programs that would begin to meet the R and D needs for Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to hear the hon. member say that he was posturing in the House. That must be a rarity. I am surprised to hear him suggest that he would ever posture. I was unaware that someone as distinguished as he, who has run to be leader of his party, would have considered indulging in such a pastime.
I did listen with interest to his comments about the past policies of the party of which I have the honour to be a member. I was amused to hear him suggest that the New Democratic Party has picked up on the policies the Liberal party began to advocate 20 years ago, in fact, almost 30 years ago.
I have always suggested that the New Democratic Party has been slow to pick up good ideas, but I did not realize it took that long.
In that vein, I wonder if the hon. member could, perhaps, say that he agrees with our party, that research and development is not the sole focus of government activity, but in fact it involves all elements of society. Much more than government is involved in it. The Liberal Party policy that has been so ably set forth in the debate today, whereby all segments of our society must participate in the development of research projects in our country is, in fact, a very sensible policy, one that commends itself to the hon. gentleman and even to the members of his party who are less up to date in their thinking than he is, 30 years back though he may be.

Mr. Speaker, there certainly is a lot to respond to in the brief question of my friend.
First of all, my friend is new to Parliament. I think he is beginning to recognize the amount of posturing that even he does automatically. At some stage he might even become so self-aware that he begins to realize that what happens on the floor of the House of Commons is one reality that in many ways is surreal to the reality of the real world.
Perhaps when he begins to realize the surreality of this place, he will become a very effective member, when he will be able to differentiate between various realities.
When my hon. friend talks about old Liberal ideas, let us not forget that the NDP is called "the Liberal Party in a hurry" by some. When I talk about the economic nationalism that used to be advocated by the Liberals, it is something that we find to be still a valid idea. If we want to follow the Liberal course in terms of how to spend money and encourage private R and D, then what Mr. Lalonde brought forward with a scientific research tax credit, saw literally billions of dollars being wasted.
March 14, 1991

I wish I had my notes on some of the research projects that the Liberals were financing at that time. I believe there was one in which they were trying to raise cows so that cows could give chocolate milk.
I believe the Liberals were going to help finance that as part of their research and development projects.
If you could run and look at the list of what the Liberals were going to sponsor-and in fact they did - billions of dollars were lost to tax scams. That is the Liberal idea of how to encourage private R and D. Well, if that is the idea, forget it. Those folks are not ready for government tomorrow. They were not ready for government then; they are not ready for government today or tomorrow, and if that is still the thinking of the Liberal Party, they are not ready for government for the next decade to come.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague for his quite helpful observations on science and technology policy. I wish my friend would not leave, because we have some words for him.
I do not think the debate here is about surrealism, quite frankly, and it may be a good deal less about posturing. I think it is about a little honesty, a little sincerity, a little seriousness, as representatives of the Canadian people.
We heard the hon. member moments ago talking about the Liberal science and technology policy of the past. I do not mind telling you, Mr. Speaker, and I know you are going to appreciate this, that the national rate of expenditures for science and technology was higher during the Diefenbaker years than it was during the Trudeau years.
When Mr. Trudeau came into office, the gross expenditure on research and development was 1.4 per cent of GDP. During the 1970s and almost throughout the 1970s it was up .9 per cent. So this party, this party which has been the firmest advocate of research and development has not a thing to learn. The Liberals could learn if they recognized the contribution they had made to the deindustrialization of Canada at the present. We are happy to see them joining the fight.
On the other hand, I just left a meeting of the Standing Committee on Industry, Science and Technolo-
Supply
gy where we sat mystified. My Liberal colleagues, whom I respect very much on that committee, heard the Minister for Science talking about an additional $1.5 billion that he had to spend, out of which there would be a number of programs launched, KAON and so on, and a number of things were somehow supposed to figure into this. I asked my colleagues where the $1.5 billion was? What is this, new money? They said, oh, no, that was the 5 per cent and the 3 per cent additions that were in the budget last year and this year.
What that means is that within the confines of a decreasing real dollar rate of expenditures for research and development, they are going to take money from already existing and short funding programs and do all of these new things. That was misleading. It was hypocritical because it communicates a bad, wrong, and unhelpful message to the people with respect to what should be done, as well as to what the government is doing.
I want to ask my hon. colleague if he thinks that so far either the Liberal Party or the Conservative Party have been essentially helpful in addressing this very desperate need of the Canadian economy.

Mr. Speaker, I think my colleague would agree that individually, members of both the Conservative Party and the Liberal Party see the importance of R and D and would like to see more R and D. However, the fact and the reality remains, that when the Liberals were in power their performance did not live up to what they publicly stated to be their goals.
Certainly the Conservative government does not live up to what even the Prime Minister has stated to be the goal. Indeed, we are slipping into a Third World stance. Of all of the OECD countries, we are one of the lowest in our expenditures on R and D as a percentage of our GDP.
In answer to my colleague, I must say honestly, no. The Liberal government and the Conservative government have not done the job which needs to be done.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to participate in the debate.

March 14, 1991
Supply
When I was reviewing the text of the opposition motion, I was struck by the fact that it failed to adequately capture the essence of the competitive technological challenge that we face.
This is a challenge which encompasses a wide range of pervasive issues, each of which is a vital element in the competitiveness equation. We are in the midst of a period of unprecedented scientific and technological change. These changes have touched every Canadian and virtually every aspect of our lives.
While research and development performance is clearly a key determinant for success, there are a number of underlying factors which we must first address. These are factors which will ultimately determine the success of any research and development effort.
One integral factor is public awareness of science and technology. It is clear that we face some rather formidable challenges in trying to build a strong science culture in this country. Changing the attitudes of a culture is a long-term process. It is an undertaking that requires the collective commitment of all sectors of our society: government at all levels, industry, organized labour, educators, parents, and our science and engineering societies and associations.
It is imperative that we make this commitment. To state it simply; if people do not properly understand what drives the changes they see happening around them, they will resist. After all, it is only human nature to do so.
The government has therefore placed the highest priority on fostering greater public awareness and understanding of science and technology. Our citizens, particularly our young people-
Spending money on advertising.

Yes, there is some advertising involved, and I am going to get to that in a moment.
Our citizens and young people must be made more aware of the integral role of scientific and technological development in our personal lives, our national economic well-being, and our international competitiveness.
We must convince more Canadians, first, that a scientifically and technologically literate workforce is a condition of continued or increasing national prosperity; and, second, that science and engineering represent very
promising careers for their children. It is vital for us to get more Canadians involved in informed debate and decision-making involving the vital science and technology issues of the day. Clearly the task at hand is a formidable one.
The message concerning the need to promote enhanced public awareness was hammered home in a survey conducted last year on Canadian scientific literacy.
The findings of this first-ever survey of adult Canadians revealed an alarmingly low level of science literacy knowledge. If there was any good news to be found in the results, it was that Canadians often scored higher than other western nations. The results of the survey were rather sobering, however. For example, over half of the respondents did not know that the earliest humans came later than the dinosaurs; close to half did not know that it takes a year for the earth to go around the sun; close to two-thirds could not name a Canadian scientist; and over half could not name a single Canadian achievement in science.
I would be curious to see how members of Parliament would score if they took the test. And I don't mean this as a commentary on the intellectual capacity of any one members but rather on the fact that our low levels of scientific literacy appear to be quite pervasive. We have our work cut out for us in terms of heightening public awareness.
We are in the midst of a period in which our nation is depending on the talents of our scientists, our technicians, and our researchers to an unprecedented extent and numbers just are not there.
A major part of our problem is attitudes, attitudes passed along from one generation to the next. Changing attitudes begins with awareness, and this applies to everybody. We need to work with our schools and our educators in more actively pursuing a range of avenues which develop science and technology literacy and prepare students for careers in these fields. We must look at options such as co-operative work education and adopt school programs which bring schools and industry together in efforts to develop the workforce of the future.
It is obvious that parents, educators, employers, and governments must take creative and concrete action to
March 14, 1991

break down the stereotypes which limit the career choices of both women and men. But government cannot do the job alone, nor should it be expected to. From a government perspective we realize that it is our responsibility to provide the leadership, the co-ordination, and the policy support needed to foster public awareness activities which involve industry, academia, and other key players.
I am proud to say that the government is committed to this leadership role. It is a strong commitment that can be traced through a number of initiatives we have launched. Hon. members have already heard or will be hearing about the Canada Scholarships Program, the Networks of Centres of Excellence and the initiatives of the Natural Sciences and Research Council. I would like to focus specifically on public awareness.
Three years ago, the government launched a national campaign to raise public awareness of the importance of science and technology to Canada's economic growth and to our quality of life. The campaign is designed to make Canadians, particularly youth, place more value on science and technology, to influence career choices, to make science and technology development an increasingly important part of public policy and to increase the level of national scientific literacy.
To date, the campaign has made significant progress towards achieving its long-term objectives. The campaign itself has developed to the point where it has become a social product for which there is a growing demand. The campaign has contributed to promoting the importance of Canadian scientific and technological development within the public issue agenda. It has begun to reverse the negative images that youth have about science, and has informed thousands of Canadians about our nation's scientific and technological achievements.
Perhaps more importantly, the science and technology public awareness campaign has helped leaders in the scientific community increase their effectiveness in communicating with the public and is both supported and catalysed provincial and territorial government action on public awareness in and outside the educational systems.
Allow me a moment to touch on some of the specific things we have done as part of the public awareness effort. We have the Science Culture Canada Program, which is supporting a wide range of projects from coast
Supply
to coast, aimed at promoting greater public awareness of science and technology.
We launched a national advertising effort aimed at youth and we produced and distributed a range of public awareness materials. A travelling, interactive computer exhibit toured shopping malls across the country. We have worked with the provinces and territories on initiatives to increase the number of science and technology-related learning experiences in elementary school classrooms.
We are working with the provinces, the teachers and the school boards to strengthen the quality of science and technology education.
It is particularly important that we reach the students in grade six through nine. Surveys have shown this to be the key period during which attitudes are shaped. It is here that we win them over or we lose them for good.
A cornerstone of our public awareness effort is National Science and Technology Week, organized jointly with the provinces and the territories and scientific and engineering groups. Last October marked the first time we focused a national spotlight on science and technology, and by all accounts the week was a great success.
We had "The Magic of Chemistry" open house in St. John's; the University of Victoria hosted the Science Olympics, where teams of high school students competed in science problem-solving contests; Yukon College hosted hands-on scientific demonstrations by guest speakers from B.C. Science World; there was a high school science award ceremony in Jonquiere, Quebec; and, Winnipeg hosted the first National Congress of Young Sciences of Canada. These are just some examples. In all, there were over 600 events held, from coast to coast, and we expect an even bigger celebration for this October.
We want to use this occasion to give young people, in fact all Canadians, an opportunity to talk to scientists, to touch technology and to explore the new ideas being discovered every day. If we can do it for fitness, for theatre or for music, then surely we can do it as well for science and technology. It is an idea whose time is long overdue.
The government would like to extend the invitation to members on all sides of the House to get involved in National Science and Technology Week. There is a great

March 14, 1991
Supply
deal we can all do in carrying the vital science and technology awareness messages to our constituencies.
I could not end without mentioning a particular science involvement in my own riding, the Edmonton Space and Science Centre. Just recently, I participated in a ceremony where the federal government committed $2 million towards that centre for the increased role that centre will be taking on as a science and learning centre in Edmonton for northern Alberta. I am happy to have that centre located squarely in the middle of my constituency.
I am pleased that I had this opportunity to outline the details of our government's significant and, indeed, unprecedented commitment to fostering the development of a science culture in Canada. It is important to note that all the policies and programs, all the grants and incentives in the world will be in vain if they are not coupled with a strong public awareness and education effort. The Government of Canada recognizes this reality and I am happy about the way that we have responded.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but say that the member who just spoke in this debate made a very interesting speech, but he avoided altogether the question and the motion which is the subject of the debate today. He started off by saying that he thought the motion was too narrowly framed in speaking of research and development, and then went on to speak about scientific literacy and scientific cultures throughout his whole speech.
I will acknowledge that the two go hand in hand, that there is a need to develop scientific culture in this country, but I find it astonishing that he did not refer to the Prime Minister's promise to double Canada's spending commitment to research and development. If the debate was too narrowly framed, his criticism should be directed to the Prime Minister, the leader of his party, who in a speech to the Montreal Chamber of Commerce seven years ago next week promised: "to double Canada's spending commitment to research and development within a first mandate".
I would like to remind him also that the Prime Minister wrote in his book Where I Stand that: "research
and development and the resulting innovations are the lifeblood of a successful economy and country".
The Prime Minister asserted that if the percentage of our Gross National Product allocated to research and development were increased by just 1 per cent, it would generate an additional one million jobs in Canada and $20 billion in additional sales of manufactured products.
Of course we know what has happened since 1984. This government has abandoned the promise made by the Prime Minister, has cut support for research and development in practically every manner possible, and as a consequence Canada's collective output to research and development has gone down, rather than go up as the Prime Minister promised seven years ago.
I would like to ask the member to say a few words about research and development. If it was so important to the Prime Minister seven years ago, why is it not a priority of the member and of this government today? Why are the jobs that would result from increased R and D spending and why are the export sales that would result from increased R and D spending not a priority of the government?
How can this member stand by while other countries are spending twice on research and development as much as Canada does and are beating the pants off us in international competition? What suggestions has he got to see that Canadian industry will spend more or invest more on research and development?
I want to anticipate the kind of point the member would probably say. I am not suggesting that the Government of Canada should throw money at the problems. Far be it for me to suggest that the Government of Canada should throw money at a problem.
What I would like from that member is some kind of an idea of how we can stimulate Canadian businesses to invest in research and development and provide Canadians with the kind of jobs and sales that they deserve and which the Prime Minister promised he would give us seven years ago?

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member answered his own question in the final two or three sentences. That is simply that it is not the question of science and technology, as he stated. I acknowledge it is a very critical one for an industrialized country like ourselves if we want to maintain our standard of living
March 14, 1991

and our living style. The fact is the equation is not simply how much money comes from the Consolidated Revenue Fund or from the taxpayers of Canada and how much money the government spends. Surely we have to look at the total industrial and scientific community of the country and we have to look not just to the government itself.
He mentioned the fact that we cannot solve the problems by throwing money at them. That is true. Perhaps I can give him two examples of things that this government did which had enormous results.
The first one is we put in place changes to the Patent Act. At the time it was called Bill C-22. I just met with somebody last week in my office from a major company which has put $100 million into research and development at the University of Alberta in Edmonton for research into pharmaceuticals and new drugs for the future. That is a $100 million investment at one university in Canada and it is directly attributable to the fact that we in the last Parliament passed that bill, I might add, fought tooth and nail by his party, his leader and by his supporters in the other place.
A second example is in northern Alberta. I will use this example because it is close to home. In northern Alberta we are going to see shortly the construction of a new forestry project. I talked with the head of the engineering firm involved with that project only last week. He was telling me that this is going to set the standard for forestry projects in the world because it will have a virtually zero emission of toxins and pollutants. He expects a lot of interest to be generated from around the world in the forestry industry by this plant which will be world class.
The Prime Minister said we needed to have increased research and development in this country, but he did not say that it had to be strictly a matter of the size of the cheque that the government would write. I think I have demonstrated through two or three examples just exactly the the kind of things we have done that are not necessarily calls upon the taxpayer.

Mr. Speaker, I am able to congratulate the member for Edmonton Northwest for his probably unsuccessful bootleg to the opposition motion put forward because let's face it the motion

put forward is a brilliant motion when we really examine it.
The member for Saint-Henri-Westmount said:
That this House condemn the Government for failing to honour the
Prime Minister's promise to "double Canada's spending commitment
to research and development."
We cannot stress enough just what the point is. The point as reported in the Gazette back on March 23,1984, said that "Mulroney promised in Montreal that a government under his leadership would bring down interest rates and double Canada's spending commitment to research and development during its first mandate", double the spending commitment, I remind the hon. member for Edmonton Northwest, in case it did not click for the last four hours. The actually quote is, and this is incredible: "We believe this will create hundreds of thousands of new jobs and billions in new sales for Canada each year". He said that to the Chamber of Commerce.
If only they had doubled the money, we would have all those jobs today.

Yes, as so articulately spelled out today in the House on a few occasions, not only during his remarks but also during his articulate pin-pointing questions to the members opposite. Contrary to the Prime Minister's promise, spending on research and development in Canada has actually gone down since the government took office and the spending commitment from close to 1.4 per cent of the gross domestic product to 1.3 per cent of the gross domestic product. That is incredible.
When did this take place? It took place probably during the most successful, resurgent years in the Canadian economy that we had seen-seven years of good fortune, of job development, of spending, of buying, of production, of jobs. And yet, down we go, to 1.3 per cent of the gross domestic product.
The member for Edmonton Northwest likes to talk about tests. The test for the member opposite is to stop with the optimistic promises for future commitments, because we have already had those. We have had these optimistic commitments to research and development for the last seven years. It is time to see his government put its money where the Prime Minister's mouth is.

The essential message is that the Liberal Party has just demonstrated again and again and again the fact that in its mind the only way to measure commitment or anything else is by how much taxpayers' money you manage to spend.
There is no point in spending money foolishly, like the $2 billion boondoggle of the SRTC.
