Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to stand here in this House today to discuss this important opposition motion.
Many of us I think can agree that research and development is the only way that we can possibly become leaders in the world, rather than be relegated to followers. It is that which permits us to find new knowledge and to apply that knowledge so that we can in fact be in the forefront in a number of areas, whether it be in the technological area or the social science and humanities.
I could talk about the promises that have been broken, but I think my colleagues have made the point several times and I won't do that, with one exception, because I find this most interesting. I want to quote from the Toronto Star an article dated January 13, 1991. It is entitled Closed Eyes on Research and Development:
For years Prime Minister Brian Mulroney has spoken eloquently and often on the need for a national commitment to research and development. In 1982, even before he became Progressive Conservative leader, Mulroney vowed to double public and private sector spending on R and D.
Here is what he said:
Either we go into the game and become important players in this major league or we become a nation that will, during its entire lifetime, play in the Junior B circuit.
He went on. In 1983 as opposition leader, he bemoaned the fact that Canada had lost-and I am quoting-"a generation because of the absence of commitment to science and technology".
What a glaring contradiction. At the end of 1984 we stood at 1.40 of gross domestic productivity. That is in terms of spending for research and development. It slipped, and it is almost 1.30 now.
People will say, and my hon. colleague said, "you measure everything with dollars". That is not the issue. The issue is that there was a promise made time and time again.
That is another lie.
And that promise was not honoured. That is what is causing a whole lot of difficulty in this country, that kind of verbal commitment, without the follow-up, without the action. It is unfortunate.
Shame.

It is easy for members to take examples of success and say: "We have built this. We have done that", but we have to look at the country and the over-all picture.
The over-all picture is not a good picture. It is simply not so. There is another technique that is being used by members of the opposition quite apart from saying that the Liberals did it or that you want to spend your way out of it. They use a number such as $40 million or $22 million. It does not really matter.
Of course, to a Canadian out there, that is a lot of money. We have to ask the other question. How much money is it in relationship of what has to be done and to what other countries are doing? If we look at those two questions, we find that it is totally inadequate.

I find it very distressing that the Prime Minister, even before he became Prime Minister, made this promise, and that later, when he should have done something, when the economic situation in Canada was still in pretty good shape-in fact it was in very good shape-he failed to support education.

We have to take a look at the cuts, the capping and all of that in the global context. Not in an unkind way, I say

that whatever the government touches in the whole area related to education and research and development, it is not going well.
The government increases the number of immigrants that it brings to this country. Bravo. That is not a real problem. But, where are the support programs? Where are the language programs? It has messed that up.
Regarding the copyright law, teachers and professors have been waiting for three years and still nothing. If I, as a teacher or professor photocopy a page or so, I have to be in fear of breaking the law. Absolutely nothing has come forward.
What about the cuts to transfer payments and $100 million to training and retraining? What about the 3 per cent administrative fee on the student aid program? What about the 7 per cent goods and services tax on books and other learning materials? I could go on and on, but we have to look at it in the global context.
It is not only the capping of research and development funds. These other reductions and cuts also have a negative impact. That is really very unfortunate.
I want to make certain that we understand the importance of research and development, not only with respect to developments in technology, but with respect to social problems in this country and indeed in this world.

So many people think that when we talk about research and development, we are talking about technological progress. Of course that is also very important, but the social sector is even more so, since the most complex problems confronting our society today are social problems.

Let me just share with you what I think most members would agree are the greatest challenges facing our nation. They are not the technological challenges. Of course, we need to make progress there. We must and we will.
What are the major challenges facing this nation? The whole question of national unity and the whole question of poverty. Almost 5 million Canadians are poor. Most of them are women and 1 million of them are children. There are 1.8 million Canadians going to food banks,
Supply
many of whom are children. There are 2 million people on welfare as we meet in this House today. There are over 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. There are 5 million to 7 million who are functionally illiterate and are costing the country a bit more than $10 billion a year.
It is really quite inappropriate that women in this country still do not have their fair share of some of the best paid positions and that they still earn roughly two thirds of what it is that men earn.
Research and development can play a role. [Translation]
Research and development must show us what we can do to correct and resolve these major problems, these major challenges to our society and to our country.

Let me say very quickly what the Royal Society has recommended. It is an important organization. It has recommended an expansion in the funding of research, the social sciences and the humanities even at a time when many observers are worried that Canada may find it difficult to keep pace with fast moving and increasingly expensive fields of research in the natural sciences, engineering and medicine. That is what the Royal Society has said with respect to social sciences.
Some will know that there are tax credits for certain types of research, but not in the social sciences. People do not see an immediate pay-off, therefore there are not the kinds of investments. Yet it is the most underfunded of all and it is probably the most important of all in terms of national unity, in terms of correcting the social difficulties which we face on a daily basis as a nation.
If we look at the government's program in terms of centres of excellence, I believe, if my memory serves me correctly, there is one on aging and its impact on society. There are literally hundreds of problems that need to be studied, yet there is only one in the centres of excellence. I think that is a powerful statement in terms of what the government sees as its priority. It is misguided.
Those are not the most important challenges facing Canada today, that is where they have invested the funds. They are important and I do not want them to lose those funds, but they must be increased in the field of social sciences and humanities. We need some tax

March 14, 1991
Supply
credits. We need some additional assistance so that we can come to grips.

Mr. Speaker, I think I have reached the end of my speech. In concluding, I would like to say that to me this is not a partisan issue. It is all about promises, promises, promises that were not kept. It is also a matter of priorities: priorities for the country, for you and me and the people we represent, for a strong, united and prosperous Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the comments of the hon. member for Saint-Boniface. When he refers to the motion which states in part, and I quote: "-the Government for failing to honour the Prime Minister's promise to 'double Canada's spending commitment to research-", I am sorry but, in our part of the country, in Abitibi and in Quebec, the Prime Minister honoured his promise. Indeed, the increase in spending was two and even threefold. Let me tell you why. In the 1991-1992 Estimates-all hon. members received a copy at their office- you can read that a new mining center will be developed this year in the North, in Quebec, at a cost of $15 million, as a site for testing ideas resulting from the mining research and development program.
Never, in the past seven years, has the Liberal Party organization in Abitibi lent a helping hand on this issue. You say that this is not a partisan matter, but you were conspicuously absent eveiytime there was an important debate. Articles such as this one are published in newspapers, and I quote: "Our thanks to the government of Canada for opening in Val-d'Or a research laboratory specializing in comminution." These are the words of our people, people like Paul Giroux, a restaurant owner, Roger Roy, from Jean Coutu pharmacy, Brigitte Giroux, from Saint-Hubert BBQ, and Roger Gareau, from Gareau Automobiles, thanking the Canadian government for developing a project for the mining sector and for helping that sector. So, are you for that project aimed at helping the mining industry in Quebec, yes or no?

Absolutely, Mr. Speaker. I am very happy that the hon. member shared with me his views and these facts, and I really like him.
But I still want to get some things straight. It is past time-as I said at the beginning of my speech-to point to some projects and figures and then try to prove something that does not exist. These projects exist. But let us look at the whole of Canada. If we look at Canada, I challenge you.
If I used any statistics that are incorrect, I am willing to do almost anything that you will ask me, dear colleague. But do not simply point to a project or a figure and then try to determine that everything works well. One other thing you have to be careful with: You said that in Quebec the spending commitment will be doubled, tripled ou quadrupled.
In Northern Quebec!

Perhaps, but some areas in Canada may have been cut, hit hard or crushed. That is what people are telling me, dear friend.
So, to summarize, I tell you that I welcome your comments. I welcome the goodwill with which you shared your views with me, but I assure you that your reality is perhaps accurate, but that mine is different, simply in that I try to think about the country as a whole, including Manitoba.

Mr. Speaker, in browsing through some of the notes, I noted that the Prime Minister complained seven years ago about the then Liberal record of percentage of GDP devoted to R and D. He was being a little cynical about it, but he said that it was 1.3 per cent of GDP. I looked at the notes from our critic today as to where the government is now in percentage of GDP applied to research and development, and it is still 1.3 per cent. We have come a long way in 28 years.
I would like to think that the process of research and development involves government, involves universities, and involves the private sector, the private sector being the clearing house. I want to comment as well that it is not simply expenditure of funds by government that is going to move this area ahead. It is actually inducements by government to the private sector to invest and spend funds. It is the over-all spending that we want to increase. We do not want it confined to government spending.
March 14, 1991

As we stand here today talking about this continuing 1.3 per cent and how we would all like to increase it, I note that we in this House have not been able to do very much about that, although we all want to.
I would like to ask my colleague whether he thinks that the social sciences which he has referred to might be able to make a contribution to the process of inducing a greater investment in R and D by all sectors of the economy.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. He has made a number of important points.
First, he has recognized the importance of social sciences. I believe that social sciences can play a meaningful role. They have been doing that, will continue to do that, and will improve on that. It is critically important that this happen. I have also indicated that there should be some tax credits for people to assist the social sciences. The member's point about getting the private sector more integrally involved in research and development is also well taken.
However, it is not just money; it is also an attitude. It is opening up our minds to the possibilities. It is recognizing that if we want to be up there as No. 1, as leaders as opposed to followers, research and development will do it for us, investment in the abilities of our people. Research and development is the key.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to share the following quote with the House in debating on this motion:
Either we go into the game and become important players in this
major league, or we become a nation that will, during its entire
lifetime, play in the Junior B circuit.
That infamous statement was made by the right hon. Prime Minister in 1982 as his way of expressing his commitment to science and technology. At that time he did not have the reins of power in his hands, but he made it clear that he intended to place Canada, through a commitment to research and development, in the major leagues.
The game remains the same. The game is cutthroat where high-tech talent and innovation translate into dollars. It is a world where the undisputed leaders have a commitment to research and development. The game remains the same, but what has happened to the commitment of the Prime Minister and his party? They have had
Supply
six years to take Canada to the major league, but we are becoming more junior every day.
As Official Opposition critic for national health and welfare, I will seize this opportunity to bring to this debate my perspective on how the government cuts are affecting health care, from lay-offs to the cancellation of research that may have shown us better and healthier lives. Unfortunately research is something that cannot be shelved now and taken out and dusted off when the economic climate is brighter.
Time does not stand still for technology. There are scientists in this country who have worked for years to gather the best people around them; specialized, talented people. I have recently heard of cases where researchers unable to realize funding from this government will have their excellent research teams disbanded. That will be a tragedy.
For instance, in the National Health Research and Development Program, estimated funding of $32 million was slashed to $28 million in the same year, in 1990. What does this mean? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, what it means to people like Dr. Raisa Deber, a professor and researcher at the University of Toronto.
Because of the uncertainty of her funding, her two junior researchers may lose their jobs. The further implication of that is that we will be losing future talents as well. Their research was a study to better treat back pain, high blood pressure and other ailments through enhanced communication with patients-excellent research protocol that may not see the light of day. Dr. Jack Siemiatycki, professor at the Institute Armand Frappier of the University of Quebec, will also be forced to let go two of his team members unless he finds the funding NHRDP no longer provides. Dr. Siemiatycki was studying the link between asbestos and cancer. Only recently in this House we have been faced with the issue of this asbestos as a source of the problem.
Additional funding is not easy to procure, I submit. Canadian companies spend on average one-half of what is spent on research and development in other industrialized countries. The government has recently turned to Canadian corporations and pointed a finger, blaming business for lack of research and development. However, the blame ought to fall on this government because this government not only has reneged on its commitment; in

March 14, 1991
Supply
fact I think it has reneged on research and development altogether.
While wishing for a high-tech economy fuelled by an educated work force that my colleague from St. Boniface has alluded to, the government pares away research funds and money for education. The government is living a catch-22, but it is the Canadian people who will be snared.
There is an apathy in the government. There is an apathy in the country. It is an apathy not shared by eight other leading industrialized countries. Canada spends only 1.3 per cent of its Gross National Product on research compared to about more than twice spent by the United States, Sweden, France, Japan and West Germany. It is no wonder Canada has fallen behind.
The National Health Research and Development Program is the main funding agency for research projects in applied health care. It is one of the most important sources of funds for researchers working for preventive medicine. Yet this agency is having its budget drained away.
Today, the climate for health care is turbulent. Transfer cuts and freezes place unprecedented pressures on provincial governments. Newfoundland's budget tried to cope by closing 360 acute care hospital beds. Nine hundred health care workers are being laid off. Quebec and Ontario, along with the western provinces are feeling the strain. Ontario spends one-third of its tax revenues on health care. Each person in this province makes on average 10 Ontario health insurance claims each year.
Recently we discussed the plight of medicare in our country. We were really saddened. Just yesterday I was discussing this issue with the member for Hamilton Mountain and the member for Mississauga East. We are really saddened. We are not seeing any future for medicare. While we recognize there is no question that the cost of health care is rising, there is no question solutions need to be found. Money needs to be found to keep medicare intact.
Yet the most promising solution, preventive medicine, is just research away.
We must learn how to prevent disease even more. We must learn how to make health care delivery more efficient.
The answer is not user fees or closing beds, as we seem to hear from the government side, and the answer definitely is not to slash the budget for research and development.
How does this government think we can defuse the problems of tomorrow unless we tackle them today? Right now, in this city, at the University of Ottawa Medical School, Dr. C. Y. Kang is developing a vaccine against the HIV virus which is known to cause AIDS. Dr. Kang's microbiology team has found a drug that stimulates immunity, the capacity for the human body to defend itself against the HIV virus and "it looks quite promising", to quote Dr. Kang. I hope, for the sake of the world, the prospect of finding funding is promising as well.
Dr. Kang will need at least $1 million to manufacture this drug properly for testing. What if the money is not available in Canada? Will doors in the United States open if Dr. Kang knocks?
Research and development are more than a means of ensuring economic prosperity; they can also be a protector. We all know the story of Banting and Best who helped discover insulin for us and, thereby, prevented a lot of misery and tragedy among patients with diabetes mellitus, patients with high blood sugar.
Through this discovery, Canadians and people around the world have been offered some respite from this illness. I believe Canadian scientists and researchers have much more to offer, if only they are allowed to pursue their talents in science.
Frequently I receive letters from people across Canada who suffer from myalgic encephalomyelitis, a type of disease that is known in layman's terms as chronic fatigue syndrome. The question is: What type of research is being done to prevent this disease? What is known about it, and how can they repair their health and lives? Maybe the government could have a better answer. I do not have the heart to tell these people that very little is being done in this country and, with the present government commitment to research and development, little will be done while this government is in power.
Let me end by echoing the sentiments of my colleague from Saint-Henri-Westmount in saying that this government should be condemned for failing to honour the
March 14, 1991

Prime Minister's promise "to double Canada's spending commitment to research and development". I challenge the government to start investing in the future that it professes to support. If we invest in the well-being of Canadians, we will have a better Canada and a better country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the member for his valuable contribution to this debate.
It is unfortunate that the Minister of National Health and Welfare chose not to intervene in this debate and respond to the comments of the member. He was referring to cuts in the budget of the National Health Research and Development Program which, as the member explained, provides funding for research to health promotion, disease prevention, health care delivery and preventive medicine.
I wondered if the member might just explain a little more what the distinction is between health care research or disease prevention and medical research, which is conducted by the MRC.

Mr. Speaker, health care research and disease prevention encompass investigations and inquiries into all aspects of health as a tool to prevent disease. One aspect of that is perhaps to help discover a vaccine that can be funded by the Medical Research Council. Other sciences, the social sciences, the role of counselling, the role of the social workers and other health care workers are all legitimate aspects of health care delivery, and we would want to know their role in preventing disease.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to follow up on my question of February 26, to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. He will know that this is no ordinary recession. Southern Ontario is being hit hard. Plants are closing down. Jobs are lost forever. It is a far cry from the temporary examples of the last recession in 1981-82.
It is a fact that only 24 per cent of the lay-offs in 1981-82 involved total or partial plant closings. But in 1990, these accounted for 64 per cent of the job cuts. I raised that issue in Question Period with the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. He basically stated that since this government had created so many jobs since 1984, there were more jobs to lose. That gives no comfort to my constituents.
For those who say that this recession is not as bad as the last one, they are dead wrong, or they have not been to southern Ontario, the economic engine of Ontario. Southwestern Ontario alone is responsible for 60 per cent of the province's gross domestic product of $250 billion.
Welfare rates in Kent county are up 400 per cent from 1981 levels. The city of Chatham has a 30 per cent unemployment rate in the automotive sector, and 38 per cent out of work in the transportation sector. These are dramatic figures, far worse than in the last recession.
For example, Motor Wheel Corporation in Chatham has been operating since I was a young child, with a labour force of over 600 strong. It is closing its doors permanently in May. Hunt-Wesson's canning plant in Tilbury made it through the last recession, doing business for over 25 years, but not this time. The company president says that the twin killers of high interest rates and the high dollar put them out of business. Now tomato farmers in my riding are left holding their baskets, with no one to sell to.
The recession is hitting hard. Dresden, with a population of 2,500 is seeing two of its major employers closing their doors, over 100 people out of work. Many of these people have worked at National Hardware, one of the firms, for over 30 years. Think of the ripple effect on the local economy. Ever since I can remember, Dresden always had about four or five farm implement dealers. Those small businessmen made it through the last

March 14, 1991
Adjournment Debate
recession, but not this time. Now there is no one left. Zero. This is no ordinary recession.
Agriculture is vitally important. Essex and Kent counties alone, grow and sell nearly half a billion dollars worth of agricultural produce. This recession is hitting us with a double whammy. While the government opposite merely says this is but a normal downturn in the economy, that by having a plant close down here and there, it somehow makes us more competitive.
About one-third of Chatham's workforce is in the auto parts industry, so it may follow that the city would suffer similar setbacks to other automotive towns, such as Oshawa and Windsor. But Chatham is smaller, with a population of only 42,000. When a plant lays off, the result devastates and disrupts the entire local economy.
Lay-offs have had a dramatic effect on the city. Real estate sales are down 50 per cent and southern Ontario merchants are not only suffering as a result of laid-off people spending less, they are also losing money to the American merchants, perhaps up to 40 per cent of their income.
Bankruptcies handled by just one office of Peat Marwick Thome in Chatham are up 50 per cent from last year. This is no ordinary recession, some mere cycle in the economy.
I was interested in the comments of the Minister for International Trade in this week's issue of Maclean's. He says the auto parts industry is mostly unskilled, and that of course we will lose some plants and workers. But he offers no adjustment programs during the restructuring. He offers no alternatives. He says to the unemployed: "You are on your own." Instead, the government fails in its commitment to research and development, and cuts and freezes education and health care.
These are not the actions of a government that is committed to training our work force for the jobs of the future or assisting those workers currently laid off.
The recession is cutting deeper into the economic foundation of southern Ontario and this government turns a blind eye to it.
We are witnessing the terrible deindustrialization of Canada. We have lost 13 per cent of all manufacturing jobs since free trade. We have lost 20 per cent of our share of the world markets during the last five years. Our segment of the world export trade fell from 5 per cent to 4 per cent. As a result our current account balance has shifted from a $2.7 billion surplus in 1984 to a $16.7 billion deficit in 1989. Our trade balance with our major trading partner, the United States, has dropped $6 billion since 1984.
As our industrial sectors are being sacked and pillaged through free trade and a sad economy, the government has offered no adjustment programs, no answers, just more of the same. Canada is facing a serious long-term competitive crisis and it is no more apparent than in southwestern Ontario.
Southern Ontario, Canada's manufacturing heartland, is suffering from hardening of the arteries. As the winds of change blow away our economic structures and erode southern Ontario's foundation, the government is just standing back and watching. Any good farmer knows that you just do not stand back and watch your soil erode and blow away. You set up windbreaks.
Our manufacturing sector is the soil by which Canada's economy grows and prospers. The Tory government is letting it erode away.
Recession is not just a word in the dictionary. It affects your neighbour across the backyard fence, the farmer down the concession road, the local coffee shop where everyone gathers at six in the morning. It affects your kid's baseball or hockey coach. Recession hits families.
To conclude, this is no ordinary recession. I will be interested in knowing what the government plans are to tune up the economic engine of southern Ontario.
Welfare rates in Kent County are zooming. Burdened by the weight of the recession, some southwestern Ontario communities, including Chatham, are eligible for the first time in history for special provincial aid to pay for skyrocketing welfare costs.
I ask the government, on behalf of my constituents and southern Ontario, what policies are in place that will lend a helping hand to workers and their families?
March 14, 1991

What is this government doing while the recession is hitting us hard? How will you assist those 64 per cent of lay-off victims who will have no factory to return to after the recession is over?

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to praise your usual patience with our colleagues in this House for the length of their speeches.
The government recognizes that the Canadian economy is going through an adjustment period, which is creating problems for many Canadians. However, considering the growth rate experienced in the past years, the slowdown should not come as a surprise. This natural consequence of rapid growth is such that the demand in products and services exceeds the economic production capacity.
The strong expansion of the Canadian economy over the past seven years has exceeded our capacity limits, both on the labour and the product markets, creating destructive inflationary pressures which threatened to settle in the economy, making their elimination more difficult and expensive as years go by.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, the government has introduced and followed fiscal and economic policies to achieve a better balance between demand and production, and to reduce inflationary pressures. These policies will lower interest rates and bring back a more balanced and sustained growth. Moreover, the government has introduced structural policies improving the competitiveness of the Canadian economy on international markets and increasing our production capacity. For instance, the imposition of the tax on goods and services allowed the Canadian manufacturing sector to improve its competitiveness, thanks to the elimination of the federal sales tax that subjected that production to discrimination, as was generally acknowledged.
Those policies aimed at reducing inflation and improving competitiveness are particularly important to protect and increase jobs in the automobile sector in Canada because of stii'fer international competition. Without a reduction in inflationary tensions in Canada, those jobs would be lost to a producer whose production costs are much lower.
Adjournment Debate
Because of the policies adopted by this government, Canada has cornered an ever larger share of the North American market.
However, the North Americain automobile industry is deep in a cyclical recession after several years of unprecedented sales that flooded the market. That recession has been aggravated by the present weakness of the economy as a whole.
We recognize, Mr. Speaker, that those periods of economic adjustment are not easy and that some people are faced with veiy real problems. However, it is important for Canadians to realize that the changing economic situation helps to ease inflationary pressures that have increased business costs and prices and that have eroded competitiveness and could jeopardize the jobs of all Canadian workers.
Also, Mr. Speaker, there are encouraging signs showing that the automobile demand may raise. In January and February, automobile sales have increased by 16 per cent over the third quarter of 1990. Because the rates have fallen by over 400 percentage points-

Mr. Speaker, the Nielsen task force which this government established several years ago did a complete review of federal government spending on housing. Its report was very revealing.
Only a fraction of the government programs in place at that time helped those in real need. Only about 40 per cent of federally-assisted housing was directed to those in need, perhaps 32,000 households.
Our government has turned this around. The new directions in housing introduced in 1986 has resulted in all social housing dollars going to those in need. Programs today are now targeted to those households that are unable to afford adequate and decent housing.
In the last four years, this government has assisted some 75,000 low income households. That is an increase of about 230 per cent over previous programs. All told, this year $1.8 billion will be spent to assist nearly 640,000 households to meet their housing needs.

March 14, 1991
Adjournment Debate
Through these subsidies, we are providing decent shelter and affordable rents. Over the lifetime of each dwelling it will provide a home to many households in their time of need. Surely these directions are the way to go.
When resources from government revenue must be carefully parcelled out, it must go to Canadians whose lives will be improved substantially. It should not be squandered on those whose personal resources are more than adequate to rent or purchase on the private market.
Studies have shown us that about 15 per cent of Canadians must rely on some form of government assistance to meet their shelter needs. I am talking about families, women with young children, the elderly, the handicapped who through no fault of their own do not have affordable homes. Many are paying 40, 50, 60 and maybe even 75 per cent of their income each month for rent and heat.
Yet there are glaring examples of well-to-do individuals who are living in housing projects that are massively subsidized by the federal government. These people are shutting out the homeless and low income Canadians from affordable housing. High income Canadians should not be taking advantage of funding intended for low and moderate income Canadians.
There is a housing co-operative in Edmonton which was given a $280,000 cash grant in 1977 when it was built. Under a special program it received a preferential mortgage rate of 8 per cent for 50 years. This means that each of the co-operative's 59 units receives a 1.5 per cent interest reduction grant of $42.83 per month.
There is an individual living in that co-op who is earning over $90,000 per year and tax-free allowances. This is completely unacceptable. This individual could easily find and afford a home to rent or buy in Edmonton. It is unconscionable that a member of this House should show so little regard for the poor of his own community. I know that there are desperate families in Edmonton who would be absolutely thrilled to have the opportunity to live in this government-assisted housing. Hi ere are at least 30 people on the waiting list to get into the Sundance Housing Co-operative in Edmonton where a member of this House resides.
Furthermore, recent statistics have come to light which make it very clear that the situation in Edmonton is not unique. There is a shocking number of people living in co-ops throughout the country who have incomes in excess of $60,000 per year, more than 12 per cent.
Many of the people living in federally subsidized housing co-ops can afford the carrying costs of a modest home. Many housing co-op projects are financed by 8 or 9 per cent mortgage money over 50 years.
Having such high income earners living in these federally assisted housing projects is an abuse of a program meant for low and medium-income Canadians. Effectively, it shuts out the homeless and needy who must have affordable housing.
I would like to return to the example of a member of this House abusing that program. The member lives in a five bedroom unit that he shares with three other adults and a teenager. The whole rent for that apartment is $622 and he is paying one fifth of that, plus a modest surcharge of $60 or $70 a month to offset some of the costs because he is in a higher category. This member should be paying market rent.
My question is: Will the minister or the parliamentary secretary and the government give consideration to either a policy of encouraging these high income Canadians who are abusing this program to move out of these co-op projects or, perhaps better yet, introducing a policy of charging the market rent so that the sum return to the community and to the government is such that we can build more units and subsidize low and moderate-income individuals.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the hon. member and his question which was directed a few weeks ago to the Minister of State for Housing.
The need for affordable housing, as he has said, is an ongoing concern and helping provide that housing is a priority of this government.
A full evaluation of the program was conducted last year. One aspect that was reviewed was the issue of high income Canadians living in co-operative housing supported by the federal government.
March 14, 1991

Last December, the minister announced that the federal government would continue with the co-operative housing program, but with some improvements. A system of income ceilings for eligibility to move into any future projects is being introduced. Once residency has been established, the household incomes will be reviewed annually.
For those households whose income goes beyond the ceiling limit, they will be surcharged. The minimum number of units in each co-operative project dedicated to households in need that benefit from rental assistance will be increased from 15 per cent to 30 per cent. Through the provinces' cost share, the Rent Supplement Program, now eight of the 10 provinces help fund up to 50 per cent of the household in each co-op.
The minister is encouraging the others to follow suit. The experimental indexed link to mortgage that has been used for the last five years has proven to be quite successful for financing co-operative housing. Efforts are under way to expand the pool of potential investors and to hopefully reduce interest costs even more.
The logical result of this change should be an increase in the number of units that can be produced each year for the same federal government investment.
I know the minister is working out the program details with the Co-operative Housing Federation. He wants to ensure that the program is as cost effective as possible while retaining a range of income. It is the responsible approach to providing affordable housing to thousands of low and moderate-income Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to expand on my concerns about the process that has been followed over a number of years not to ensure the environmental soundness of a project called the Rafferty-Alameda dam.
This has been a sorry history at every stage of ministers of the Crown putting their political concerns for friendly relations with certain premiers above the concerns of Canadians for their environment, for the protection of their water supply and for a number of other serious concerns about the ecosystems of Canada.
Adjournment Debate
Time after time we have heard in this House statements from ministers that they want to see a full environmental assessment, but the actions have not matched those statements. This week we have had the Rawson Academy of Aquatic Sciences make a submission to the Environmental Assessment Panel reviewing a project that is, for all intents and purposes, well on its way to completion and therefore not even amenable to controls on how it is developed to bring those more in conformity with the best interests of protecting the environment.
As I look over the agreement that the Rawson academy analysed this week for the Environmental Assessment Panel, I think I see some of the problems as to why the ministers in this House have spoken positive words and taken very little action. This agreement signed in 1959 guarantees that the Government of Canada will expeditiously provide the Government of the United States of America with a minimum of a certain amount of flood storage. It is not as surprising as it might have been at the time, when we see the minister promising action and taking none.
We will recall that it took two court cases to order the Minister of the Environment to carry out an environmental assessment and that even then the actual establishing of that environmental assessment was delayed by up to eight months before it commenced. By that time, as we well know, there were suspicions about secret agreements behind closed doors, with the premier of Saskatchewan to give a nod and a wink and let the construction of the Rafferty Dam and the beginning of Alameda Dam proceed despite there being no environmental assessment.
We now know that Rafferty is virtually complete, that Alameda is well under way, and that no environmental assessment has been completed, so it is impossible to correct the design or construction of those dams to conform with the interests of the environment.
What was not quite so clear is that we are not even able to put environmental constraints on the operation of those dams. The environmental panel which we thought at least had the ability to recommend that the dams be operated in an environmentally positive way, or at least in a minimally damaging way, would not even have the ability to make those recommendations because the ability of the Government of Canada to control the operation is already seriously compromised by an agree-

March 14, 1991
Adjournment Debate
ment it entered into with the United States for the operation of the dam, by the operating agreement that is attached to that, and by a licence that has been issued which relates to the operation of the dam.
Two ministers this week have tried to assure the House that despite the analysis by the Rawson academy the control of water relating to these dams is under the jurisdiction of a 1959 intergovernmental agreement and under the control of the International Joint Commission. Nothing could be further from the truth because this agreement in fact modifies that 1959 agreement. The International Joint Commission has not even been advised that that agreement has been changed, nor has it been told that its mandate under it has changed. Even though it recommended that 1959 agreement for the apportioning of water between Saskatchewan and North Dakota, it was not consulted on amendments to it, nor will it be consulted on agreements still to be made as to the water quality.
Lest we question who this agreement is in the interest of, I would like to quote a few sections of it:
- releases from the Canadian dams will be scheduled to coincide with the periods of beneficial use in North Dakota -may be delayed when the State of North Dakota determines and notifies Saskatchewan-
Saskatchewan shall deliver water "if North Dakota requests the delivery".
The International Joint Commission for many years has functioned to protect water quality and water distribution between Canada and the United States. It is not too late to bring that body into a review of this agreement, a review of the water quality standards which must be set before April 1 of this year, and to ensure that the International Joint Commission with all its expertise is in fact reviewing this agreement and is making recommendations so that it will operate in the best interests of Canada.
Piece by piece this country is giving away control over its own water. We are constructing dams with no national control over the ultimate and cumulative effect of those dam. We already have more water diversions in Canada than the United States and the U.S.S.R. combined, and
we have no idea what the ecological effects of those diversions are.
It is not too late for the national government to take control of the most important national resource we have, and that is water. The government itself in its federal water policy had good words to say about the importance of the control of quantity and quality of water in Canadian hands. Where it has had the opportunity to exercise that control in case after case, it has failed to do so. It has failed to ensure that an environmental assessment is conducted to protect the quality and quantity of water for Canadians.
I urge the government to revise this agreement to make sure that it is doing what it should be doing for Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member opposite for Ottawa West has raised questions with respect to the latest development on the Rafferty-Alameda project in south eastern Saskatchewan.
As the Minister of the Environment indicated earlier, proceeding with additional construction of the Rafferty Dam and additional components such as the Alameda Dam and the interconnecting channel between Rafferty and Boundary Reservoirs would be in direct contravention of the Canada-Saskatchewan agreement which was designed to respect the integrity of the environmental assessment and review process.
In response to the hon. member's specific question as to whether contracts for the Alameda Dam were let or not, officials of the Department of the Environment have informed the minister that bids for a contract were in fact received, some land acquisition actions were initiated by the Saskatchewan government and technical review is now under way.
I sense that receiving the bids and land acquisitions by the province are clear statements of the province's intention to go ahead with the construction of the Alameda Dam, which were certainly not permitted by the agreement of January 26.
The latest field observation confirmed that there is limited construction activity on the Alameda site indicating some parts of the contracts were already let by the Saskatchewan government.
March 14, 1991

The Government of Saskatchewan must respect the Canada-Saskatchewan agreement which arose as a result of the Federal Court order of December 28, 1989. That order requires an environmental assessment by an independent panel according to the federal guidelines order for the environmental assessment and review process. In keeping with that, the Minister of the Environment appointed a panel on February 5, 1991 under the guidelines order in response to the court order.
Furthermore, as the minister indicated earlier, the province is proceeding with extended activities on the project beyond the scope that was agreed upon with the January agreement for which Canada offered financial assistance to the province. The concern that has been highlighted by the member is also shared by the minister. As a first step the Minister of the Environment has ordered that the payments to Saskatchewan be withheld until we are satisfied that the province is living up to the agreement.
Adjournment Debate
As the hon. Minister of the Environment stated in the House on October 18, Environment Canada officials have been instructed to seek an injunction against the province on continued construction and land acquisition related to the Rafferty-Alameda project. The Minister of Justice has agreed to initiate such action immediately following denial of the government's request for an injunction by the provincial Justice McPharson on November 15, 1990. An appeal process is under way.
Our laws must be respected and it is the government's intention to see that it happens anywhere in this great country of ours, regardless of which province.
